Artificial intelligence shopping assistants employed by Amazon and Walmart are capable of detecting false "Made in USA" product labels, but the retail giants are reportedly not utilizing this technology to crack down on misleading listings, according to a new study.

The research, conducted by a think tank led by former U.S. Federal Trade Commission Chair Lina Khan, reignites concerns about the conflicting incentives of AI shopping assistants, which retailers primarily view as tools to boost consumer spending.

Amazon's Alexa for Shopping and Walmart's Sparky assistants can identify discrepancies between explicit "made in USA" claims and contradictory information found within product descriptions, the study's authors noted.

When researchers queried the AI bots about their companies' inaction on false labeling, the chatbots offered business justifications. Walmart's Sparky, for instance, responded that the FTC typically enforces "made in USA" rules against manufacturers, not retailers.

Amazon's Alexa for Shopping and Walmart's Sparky assistants can identify discrepancies between explicit "made in USA" claims and contradictory information found within product descriptions ( Justin Sullivan/Getty Images )

"That's a business calculation, not a legal justification," Walmart's chatbot said, according to the study.

A spokesperson for Walmart did not immediately comment.

"Country-of-origin information, when available, is currently displayed on product detail pages, and we’re continually working to improve Alexa for Shopping’s ability to accurately provide this information to make it even more accessible for customers,” a spokesperson for Amazon said.

Amazon takes action when it finds sellers violating its policies, the company added.

The study is the first published by Columbia Law School's Center for Law and the Economy, launched after Khan returned to the university after her stint with the Federal Trade Commission.

"Even as AI tools continue to grow in sophistication and capability, business incentives will shape how these advancements get deployed. Policymakers and enforcers have a vital role to play to ensure the public doesn't get the short end of the stick," Khan said.

FTC rules require products advertised as "made in USA" to be "all or virtually all" made in the United States. The FTC last year urged Walmart and Amazon to crack down on third-party sellers' "made in USA" claims, citing company policies requiring sellers to provide accurate information.

When asked about false "made in USA" claims persisting on the platform, Amazon's Alexa replied, according to the authors, "The harm to U.S.-made brands is real and documented, but until that harm creates a financial, regulatory, or reputational cost for Amazon specifically, it remains easier to do nothing."

Khan sued Amazon when she was at the FTC, accusing it of holding illegal online retail monopolies. The case is ongoing.

Americans outside the nation's capital will soon be able to get limited-edition U.S. passports that feature a picture of President Donald Trump and celebrate America’s 250th birthday, the State Department said Thursday.

The department’s 27 passport agencies nationwide will start offering the special travel documents next month. They previously had only been available at the Washington, D.C., passport office for in-person applicants.

Trump, whose stern portrait is emblazoned on an inside page, is the first living president featured in the travel document.

The passports are the latest instance of Trump having his name and likeness added to buildings, documents and other highly visible tributes. His image is on a gold-finished commemorative coin celebrating the country’s founding that the U.S. Mint has begun producing, and there are efforts to put Trump’s signature on all new U.S. paper currency, also a first for a sitting president.

“In response to overwhelming demand, the Department of State is making an additional 250,000 of the special commemorative passports available to the public,” it said in a statement. “Americans all across the country will now have the opportunity to apply for one of these additional special passports, known as the ‘Patriot Passport.’”

Passport offices in Centennial, Colorado; Chicago; Dallas; Detroit; New Orleans; New York; and Stamford, Connecticut, will offer the Trump passports at one-day special events starting Aug. 8. The list will grow to include other passport offices throughout August.

Those who want the special passport must apply in-person on the day specified on the department’s passport website. Those wanting a traditional passport must apply on different days.

The commemorative passport features Trump’s picture over a gold imprimatur of his signature to an interior page, while the cover carries the words “United States of America” in bold gold print at the top and “Passport” at the bottom — a reversal of the current standard cover.

In addition, a small gold laminate American flag, with the number 250 encircled by stars, is at the bottom of the back cover.

The only presidents featured in current U.S. passports are in a double-page depiction of Mount Rushmore in South Dakota — George Washington, Thomas Jefferson, Theodore Roosevelt and Abraham Lincoln.

Other depictions include the Statue of Liberty, the Liberty Bell and Independence Hall in Philadelphia, and scenes of the Great Plains, mountains and islands. Current passports also contain quotations from Martin Luther King Jr. as well as Presidents Washington, Jefferson, Roosevelt, John F. Kennedy and Dwight Eisenhower.

The addition of Trump’s picture and signature to the passport book is the newest step his aides have taken to increase the president’s visibility, including adding his name to the U.S. Institute of Peace building and the Kennedy Center performing arts venue, although that signage was later removed on a court order.

Trump also has made waves with his plans for a new White House ballroom and a massive arch to be built at one of the entrances to Washington from Virginia.

“What a nice song,” said President Donald J. Trump, as he wandered to a podium set up outside the White House with God Bless the USA blaring over loudspeakers. He was here to promote a very normal, fairly standard Republican policy: jobs for veterans (in this case, driving trucks.)

It would allow him to rant about immigrants a little bit and to claim that he was taking back the economy stolen by “illegal aliens” and giving it to the most deserving of all Americans, service members. So far, so conservative.

What today’s event actually revealed about his own frailty and the behavior of the people around him, however, was interesting ... and a little unsettling.

Trump was reading from a piece of paper in front of him for this entire appearance, but when he did attempt to go off-script, it went very quickly awry. This policy is for “the amazing veterans who are with the — with, with us — they’ve just been with us from the day they were born, I suspect,” he said, in a trailing aside.

It was pure nonsense, even by the standards of Trump. It was so weird that I had to listen to it back to make sure I'd heard what I thought I'd heard.

open image in gallery ( Reuters )

“American highways and roadways have been terrorized” by immigrant drivers, he continued, who were driving “big rigs. Rigs like that—” At this point, a large truck caught his eye and he continued, “—Wow, that sucker is a big one. That’s big stuff.”

Trump is known for peppering his speeches with such interruptions, but these had a low energy to them and an undercurrent of confusion. Sure, he could read out from the paper that “radical left maniacs” have given out commercial licenses to people here illegally, and claim that an immigrant from Haiti who caused the death of an American citizen was “let in by Joe Biden.” But when he needed to elaborate, he could only say that such aliens had caused “many, many deaths, too many to talk about.”

The message seemed clear: Donald Trump is tired.

Luckily, transportation secretary Sean Duffy was there to add his own two cents. Jumping in with vigor, Duffy painted a suitably horrifying picture of the vulnerable American family being preyed upon by evil, English-eschewing migrants with designs on their two most sacred activities, Christian worship and mass consumption: “When these illegals were driving these big rigs, they were killing American citizens,” he yelled.

Whether you were “a family going to Walmart or going to church on a Sunday,” you were liable to be run down at every turn. Duffy had the energy Trump lacked; indeed, Trump used to be good at fear-mongering like this at rallies. Not any more.

Duffy then took a short detour into claims that President Biden didn’t allow background checks, before attempting to bring things back around to something resembling bipartisanship by stating: “There’s a lot of things that the radical left get angry about, because they’re radical, but safety is a bipartisan issue.”

open image in gallery Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy was effusive in his praise of boss Donald Trump — as we’ve come to expect, but this event revealed something more about the president ( AFP/Getty )

Perhaps the most telling moment was when Duffy wrapped up his speech, placed his hand on his heart and said to the president, “I am grateful for your leadership.” Facing the crowd and cameras again, he underlined how Trump and only Trump has put “American roads first over the illegals who the last administration prioritized.”

“It has been just an honor to work with you,” Duffy continued, as he looked back to the president, before telling the room that Trump was really a “masterclass” in himself, and that “to watch him and learn from him is amazing.”

This extended show of fealty — which took up almost as much time as the talk about opportunities for veterans — earned Duffy a nod from the president, and presumably protected him from his ire. But this, combined with the frail delivery from Trump, pointed to something alarming: a president who increasingly loses his train of thought, who struggles to make the quick quips and connections he once did, and a surrounding team that is sycophantic to the point of absurdity.

It’s pretty obvious that there isn’t just a lack of pushing-back within the Trump cabinet; there’s a demand for time-wasting, toadying displays of OTT loyalty. There’s also clearly pressure to look the other way, to paper over the cracks when the president flounders.

The ‘Freedom Haulers’ thing, by the way, is nothing new. It’s simply an extension of an older policy, and there’s very little proof that it will do much for the economy, for immigration, or for veterans. But listen, the amazing veterans have been with us since the day they were born, and Donald Trump is a masterclass. Hand on heart, is there anything more you need to hear than that?

News.title: World Cup boycott latest: Uefa confirm action with statement slamming Gianni Infantino sell-off plan
News.content:
Fifa's World Cup plan is worse than the Super League

Uefa will boycott the World Cup and all Fifa competitions if Gianni Infantino’s controversial plans to sell off stakes in its major tournaments to external investors are voted through.

“Uefa and its 55 member associations stand as one,” a statement said following an emergency Uefa meeting on Thursday. “We unanimously and unequivocally reject Fifa’s proposal to transfer ownership interests in the World Cup and other Fifa competitions to private investors.

“The World Cup cannot be treated as an investment product. It is one of football’s greatest sporting legacies. It has been built over generations by players, national teams and supporters across every continent. No part of it should ever be surrendered to private investors. The World Cup is not for sale. As a result of today’s discussion, no Uefa national teams will participate in any Fifa competition for so long as these proposals remain alive, unless this proposal has been abandoned in its entirety and binding assurances have been given that Fifa will never again open its governance or competitions to private ownership.”

Uefa were left dismayed that Infantino has given Fifa’s member associations just 53 days to decide their position and were outraged by Infantino promising a $40m (£30m) windfall to nations who back the proposals, or have the one-off payment withdrawn. Uefa’s statement added: “National associations around the world are now presented with an ultimatum: accept the irreversible capture of football’s greatest competitions or bear the consequences. This is not a ‘democratic decision’, but governance by intimidation – an act of coercion unworthy of an institution entrusted with the stewardship of the global game.”

A spokeswoman for the English FA echoed the Uefa sentiment, saying: “We stand shoulder to shoulder with our European colleagues and fully support the collective view. We oppose Fifa’s plans – the Fifa World Cup belongs to football and always will.”

Uefa previously said that Infantino’s plans to sell off stakes in Fifa’s major tournaments to private investors, including members of Donald Trump’s family, “crossed a line”. Uefa also knows it will require support from another confederation to block Infantino’s plans, as Fifa only requires a majority (50 per cent plus one) vote from its 211 member associations – though Concacaf have officially rejected the proposals as pressure builds on the Fifa president.

One of Scouting America's biggest gatherings has eliminated dedicated spaces for gay youth, women and scouts of color as the organization faces pressure from the Pentagon to pull back diversity efforts.

The changes at the National Jamboree, which ends Friday, reflect shifts made by Scouting America since the organization became a target of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over what he calls “woke” policies. Some scouts who had planned to attend the event in West Virginia said they backed out because Scouting America scrapped the inclusion initiatives it previously celebrated.

Hegseth threatened to end the Pentagon's century-old partnership with Scouting America if it did not make changes including refocusing away from diversity initiatives. The organization, previously known as Boy Scouts of America, rebranded in 2024 to emphasize inclusion and the growing number of girls in the scouting ranks.

“Scouting fundamentally is a safe place for young people to have fun,” said Samuel J. Aronson, an assistant scoutmaster who has organized inclusive events at previous national events. “In the absence of these spaces, we’re denying all that, both the safety and the fun, to thousands of young people.”

Thousands attend the National Jamboree

This year, about 15,000 scouts, leaders and volunteers from across the country are attending the 10-day event in the mountains of West Virginia. In addition to activities including mountain biking and kayaking, the gathering hosts leadership programs and educational sessions.

A Scouting America spokesperson said the organization remains “fully committed to welcoming and serving all youth,” but did not address questions about the changes to the jamboree.

The Pentagon made a deal with Scouting America in February but the two sides have given conflicting accounts of that agreement. This month, a gay rights activist obtained the memo outlining the agreement from the Defense Department after filing a lawsuit, arguing that clarity was of public importance.

The six-page document spells out ways the Pentagon will monitor compliance, including that officials from each organization would have “periodic touchpoints and meet” as needed. It was obtained by James Dale, who was expelled from the Boy Scouts in the early 1990s for being gay and later sued over discrimination. He equated the Pentagon's tactics to the actions of a bully.

“They basically have their thumb on the organization, threatening them under constant pressure,” Dale said.

Deal preserves ties between Scouting America and Pentagon

The scouts and the military have long held close ties; The military provides logistical support for the jamboree and some scout troops meet on or near bases.

Asked about the implementation and monitoring of the deal, a Pentagon spokesperson referred to previous comments by Hegseth.

In February, Hegseth posted a video that said his department would “vigorously review” changes made by Scouting America and would cease the military’s longtime support of the organization if it failed to comply by late August.

Some scouts disappointed by changes to inclusion efforts

John Andrew Segebarth, a 21-year-old college student and Eagle Scout, has been disheartened by the agreement. He joined the scout ranks in first grade and said he had been looking forward to staffing the space for LGBTQ+ and Allied Scouts at this year’s Jamboree.

Segebarth, who is gay and was elected by peers as a national officer for scouts in 2024, said the removal of inclusive spaces is a sharp reversal for Scouting America. National scouting events in recent years included community spaces for girls, scouts of color, LGBTQ+ scouts and persons with disabilities, according to Aronson.

“Scouting’s kind of walking back on its values that they told me they believed in,” said Segebarth who, along with Aronson, decided not to attend the jamboree this year.

It was at a community tent that Layla Grace found the first place where she could talk openly about being a transgender female. Now a 21-year-old assistant scoutmaster, Grace had also planned to staff the space for LGBTQ+ and Allied Scouts in West Virginia this year.

When the spaces were canceled, Grace said she almost didn't go to the jamboree but decided she wanted to be there to help those in need. She wound up volunteering at an area dedicated to addressing issues that include mental health, food security and education.

And she's trying to fill the gap left by the removal of inclusive areas.

“I am wearing so many rainbows on me, my right hand has my nails painted in the lesbian flag and my left hand has my nails painted in the transgender flag,” she said. “I am being as loud as I can to do my best to hopefully make up for the lack of community spaces.”

___

Associated Press reporter Ben Finley contributed to this report from Washington.

News.title: Computers can leak secrets without being hacked - and with new tech comes new side channel attacks
News.content:

When people hear the word cyberattack, they usually imagine someone guessing a password, planting malware, stealing a computer, hacking an organization’s network or exploiting a flaw in software. A side-channel attack works differently. It looks for clues a computer gives away while doing ordinary work.

A simple analogy is a locked safe. A thief may not know the combination and may not be able to break the lock. But if the thief can listen closely as the dial turns, small clicks or churns or pauses might reveal something about what is happening inside. The safe is not meant to share that information, but its physical behavior still leaks clues.

Modern computers have their own versions of such clues. For example, each computer might take different amounts of time to complete different tasks or may use different amounts of electricity. The hardware – processors, memory, graphics cards and storage drives – may leave tiny patterns as they work.

I’m a computer scientist who studies security and privacy. I define a side-channel attack as an attempt to observe these indirect clues and use them to infer something private.

Side-channel attacks are a reminder that computers do not have to intentionally reveal secrets to leak them. Sometimes the smallest clues left behind while they work can say more than anyone expected ( Getty Images )

This is what makes these side-channel attacks unusual. The weakness comes from the way a machine performs its work. The attacker does not steal a password directly or break into the computer, but instead studies the traces left behind by the machine while it is operating.

History of leaking

The idea is not new. In 1985, Dutch researcher Wim van Eck showed that electromagnetic signals from video display units could be captured and decoded, raising the possibility of eavesdropping on what a screen displayed. The screen was not intentionally broadcasting its contents. It was leaking signals as a side effect of operating.

In the 1990s, side-channel attacks became especially important in cryptography, the science of protecting information. In 1996, cryptography researcher Paul Kocher showed that carefully measuring how long certain operations took could reveal private information from systems using common cryptographic methods. A few years later, Kocher and fellow cryptographers Joshua Jaffe and Benjamin Jun showed that measuring power consumption could help recover secret keys from tamper-resistant devices such as smart cards.

These discoveries changed how engineers thought about security. It was not enough to ask whether an encryption algorithm was mathematically secure. It was even more important to ask whether the device running the algorithm leaked hints through timing, power, sounds or other physical behavior.

There are several common types of side channels:

A timing attack looks for small differences in how long operations take.

A power attack studies electricity use.

Electromagnetic attacks examine unintended signals.

Acoustic attacks use sound.

In one striking example, researchers showed that the faint noise produced by a laptop during certain cryptographic operations could be used, under experimental conditions, to extract a 4,096-bit secret cryptographic key.

The examples that brought side-channel attacks into wider public discussion were processor attacks. Modern computer processors such as CPUs are extremely fast because they predict what a program is likely to do next. This technique, known as speculative execution, helps computers run more efficiently. But in 2018, cybersecurity researchers discovered two vulnerabilities, dubbed Meltdown and Spectre, in the technique. They showed that these predictions could leave behind measurable traces. A malicious program could use those traces to learn information that should have been protected from it.

Meltdown and Spectre mattered because they challenged one of the basic premises of modern computing: that different programs running on the same machine should be kept separate. They also showed that performance features built deep into computer chips could have security consequences.

New tech, new side channels

Since then, researchers have continued to find new side-channel attacks in modern hardware. One such side-channel attack revealed in 2022, called Hertzbleed, showed that changes in processor frequency – normally used to save power and manage performance – could become a timing signal that could, in some cases, expose remote servers’ cryptographic secrets.

Another side-channel attack, dubbed Downfall and revealed in 2023, affected certain Intel processors. It showed how a feature called Gather could leak older pieces of data left inside the processor after earlier work. Zenbleed, also revealed in 2023, affected AMD Zen 2 processors and could allow sensitive information from another process to appear where it should not.

About the author Chetan Jaiswal is an Associate Professor of Computer Science at Quinnipiac University. This article was first published by The Conversation and is republished under a Creative Commons licence. Read the original article.

Side-channel research has also moved beyond CPUs. GPU.zip showed that graphics processors, or GPUs, can sometimes leak visual clues through the way they handle image data behind the scenes, including the pixels from another webpage in the Google Chrome browser. GoFetch, published in 2024, showed that a hardware feature in many Apple processors designed to predict future memory needs could undermine protections in cryptographic software and help extract secret keys.

The latest attack, called FROST, short for “fingerprinting remotely using OPFS based SSD timing,” involves solid-state drives, or SSDs. These drives are an extremely common form of fast storage on almost all modern computers. FROST shows that a malicious website can use a browser storage feature called the origin private file system to create and access files inside a protected area, called sandbox, that the browser sets aside for that website, then measure tiny delays in SSD activity.

The intuition is simple. If several programs are using the same storage device, they can slow one another down slightly, like cars sharing the same road. By measuring those delays in a browser, the FROST researchers showed that a website could, under specific conditions, infer information about other activity on the same computer, such as websites visited or applications used.

Lessons more than losses

So, how often are side-channel attacks used? The honest answer is that while they can be damaging, they are not the everyday cyberattack most people encounter. Most real-world cybercrime still relies on easier and cheaper methods, such as exploiting software vulnerabilities, stealing credentials, phishing, malware and ransomware. Verizon’s 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report, for example, highlights software vulnerabilities and ransomware as major sources of breaches, not side-channel attacks as a routine entry point.

This does not make side-channel attacks unimportant. Many are discovered by researchers before they are seen in widespread criminal use. But they matter because they expose weaknesses in the assumptions behind modern computing. They influence chip design, browser security, cloud computing, cryptographic libraries and the way engineers think about privacy.

Side-channel attacks are a reminder that computers do not have to intentionally reveal secrets to leak them. Sometimes the smallest clues left behind while they work can say more than anyone expected.

Top university graduates in math and computer science are landing starting pay packages worth up to a million dollars as AI companies and Wall Street trading firms fight over the same small group of specialists.

The salary jump is being driven by trading firms shifting toward machine learning and large language models. That shift puts Wall Street in direct competition with AI labs like OpenAI and Anthropic, which are all trying to hire from the same small group of experts.

“The delineation is pre-OpenAI and post-OpenAI,” Matt Stabile, founder of the recruitment firm Stabile Search, told The Wall Street Journal. “That’s when you saw competition really take off.”

Stabile noted that while seven-figure packages for early-career hires used to be rare anomalies, “a million dollars is something people don’t even bat an eye at anymore.”

Standard baseline packages at top trading shops typically land between $350,000 and $500,000, but recruiters say those numbers jump quickly. In some cases, portfolio managers bypass typical pay structures to secure top summer interns before they enter the job market.

open image in gallery Top mathematics and computer science university graduates are landing starting pay packages worth up to a million dollars as AI companies, such as Anthropic, and Wall Street trading firms fight over them ( Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images )

“They happen to intern for a highly successful person on a highly profitable desk who wants to take them off the market,” Kevin Cassata, founder of executive-search firm Karbon Agency, told the publication. “They’ll just say, ‘OK, here’s your return offer — it’s $700,000.’”

Cassata said he had seen entry-level offers top out at $1.5 million, comparing the current market to free-agency bidding wars in professional sports.

The financial scale of these firms allows them to rival major tech companies. In the first quarter of 2026, quantitative trading firm Jane Street generated $10.3 billion in profit, roughly double the earnings of Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley combined, despite operating with a fraction of their workforce.

To secure talent early, firms start outreach well before college graduation.

Optiver, a leading quantitative firm, sponsors chess grandmasters, runs campus events and flies students to its offices. The company currently fills 70 percent of its graduate roles through its internship programs and plans to eventually source all entry-level hiring through that channel.

open image in gallery The salary jump is being driven by trading firms shifting toward machine learning and large language models. That shift puts Wall Street in direct competition with AI labs like OpenAI ( Getty Images )

“Outstanding people are in more demand than they’ve ever been, and that does create competitive pressure on wages,” Charlie Whitmer, Optiver’s U.S. chief operating officer, told The Wall Street Journal. “As competition increases for outstanding people, prices naturally rise.”

Students frequently cite high compensation and faster feedback as primary reasons for choosing trading over traditional research.

Andrew Lai, who completed a doctorate in computer science at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology before joining Optiver full-time, told the publication that he preferred the field because it allowed him to see the practical results of his research quickly.

Lai noted that about a third of his doctoral lab mates entered quantitative finance, while an equal share went into tech.

“Comp was a big factor,” Daniel Wu, a Stanford computer science graduate who joined a quantitative firm in 2021, told The Wall Street Journal. “At the time, quant firms were making the most competitive offer financially.”

However, the lucrative packages are also diverting talent away from academia.

At Oxford University’s Mathematical Institute, summer internships offering upwards of $30,000 a month frequently convince doctoral students to abandon academic career plans. Graduates entering the field typically secure packages between $300,000 and $1 million, with those specialized in large language modeling landing at the top of that range.

“Once they have a taste of what it means to work for these firms and the amount of money they could be making, the majority of them would rather go into industry,” Alvaro Cartea, an Oxford math professor and director of the Oxford-Man Institute, said. “All I’m saying is that temptation is extremely strong.”

News.title: UK economy to flatline, warns Bank of England
News.content:
Britain’s economy is set to almost grind to a halt for the rest of the year, the Bank of England has warned.

Growth will drop to just 0.1pc per quarter, the Bank predicted, slowing sharply after a strong start to 2026.

Higher petrol prices and energy bills, a weak jobs market and rising mortgage costs are all draining confidence and spending power from the economy.

Inflation, which slowed to a 15-month low of 2.6pc in June, is also expected to rise again to 3.2pc later this year, the Bank warned.

Andrew Bailey, the Bank’s Governor, said inflation had “fallen faster than we’d expected” but warned that war in the Middle East would lead to a fresh spike.

He added that growth would “weaken slightly further in the near term as the effects of the conflict weigh further on demand”.

The Bank also predicted that unemployment will rise back above 5pc in the coming months, limiting workers’ ability to ask for higher wages to cope with rising living costs.

It presents a challenging backdrop for Andy Burnham and his Chancellor, John Healey, who have pledged to help voters struggling with the cost of living.

The forecasts came as policymakers led by Mr Bailey held interest rates at 3.75pc.

Although three members of the nine-strong Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) voted for higher rates, up from two at the previous meeting, the Governor dismissed suggestions the Bank is moving towards higher interest rates.

The public should “not… [think] the Bank of England is edging towards a hike,” Mr Bailey said.

“Frankly there is nothing I have said, or any of us have said, along those lines. We took a decision today to leave the Bank Rate unchanged and that is the relevant conclusion.”

Clare Lombardelli, a Deputy Governor, said voting to keep rates at 3.75pc “was not a close judgement”, calling the decision “pretty clear” given slowing inflation in the domestic economy.

Officials are monitoring the economy for any signs that increases in oil, gas and petrol prices caused by the war in Iran are creeping into higher costs and wages in the wider economy.

Mr Bailey said: “The possibility of repeated resumptions of conflict, combined with lower than usual European gas stock levels and a fall in global refining output, mean that risks to energy prices lie to the upside.”

He added: “Reassuringly, there are few signs so far that second-round effects are generating more broad-based inflationary pressures.”

Companies are struggling to pass higher costs on to their customers because of the economy’s weakness, he added.

Workers are typically securing only modest pay rises as the weak jobs market leaves them in a poor position to push for bigger salaries.

Mr Bailey stressed there are still major risks to the outlook given the war and promised to “monitor the situation carefully” and was “ready to adjust our stance”.

“It is our job to ensure that inflation gets back to the 2pc target and stays there, and that is what we will do,” he said.

Borrowing costs dropped in financial markets after the decision.

The Government’s two-year borrowing cost fell from 4.44pc to 4.34pc, the sharpest fall in a month.

The FTSE 250 index of mid-sized UK companies rose 0.8pc to a record high of 24,184.10.

Traders still believe the Bank will raise interest rates twice within a year.

However, Paul Dales, chief UK economist at Capital Economics, said rate rises “remain more a threat than a reality”.

He said there was evidence of disinflation in the economy and interest rates could be “cut to 3pc in 2027”, adding: “That’s very different to market pricing for rates to be close to 4.5pc in 2027.”

News.title: Arsonists torch more Ebola clinics as misinformation spirals in DRC
News.content:
Two more Ebola treatment facilities have reportedly been burned down in recent days as health officials struggle to overcome violent public mistrust of medical teams.

At least a dozen facilities have now been attacked since Congo declared its Ebola outbreak amid fear, misinformation and suspicion of outside authorities.

The outbreak is the fastest growing on record and officials said the virus had now killed more than 1,500 people.

The official death toll from the outbreak centred on the north eastern Ituri province of Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) has risen by 500 in only a week.

Sources told the Telegraph the large jump in deaths was largely caused by a “data harmonisation exercise” between different regions, and the new deaths may not have all happened in the past week.

However, the daily confirmed toll has also continued to climb sharply with the latest government update reporting 50 people dying in the previous 24 hours.

Airfinity, a health analytics firm, said the outbreak “continues to outpace detection and the response” and there is a high chance of it spreading further inside DRC.

News.title: Race for vaccine against new Ebola strain gets $8.5m boost
News.content:
The “most promising” vaccine to tackle the Ebola strain behind an explosive outbreak in the Congo has been given an $8.5 million boost, as researchers race to develop an effective shot.

So far at least 3,360 people have been infected and 1,487 people have died in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), in an epidemic triggered by the Bundibugyo species of Ebola.

But unlike past outbreaks of the more common Zaire strain, there are currently no approved vaccines to tackle Bundibugyo.

On Thursday, the Coalition of Epidemic Preparedness Innovations (Cepi) revealed up to $8.5 million of funding for the only single-dose inoculation, which was described as the “most promising vaccine candidate” by the World Health Organization (WHO) in an analysis in May.

It is being developed by researchers at Hilleman Laboratories – a unique partnership between the pharmaceutical giant Merck and the British philanthropic powerhouse Wellcome, which is headquartered in Singapore.

The vaccine candidate is a Bundibugyo version of the Ervebo shot, which was created by Merck (MSD in Europe) and has already been approved for Ebola Zaire.

It uses a rVSV platform, where a modified version of VSV virus is used to train the immune system to react to target pathogens – in this instance, the Bundibugyo species replaces Zaire.

News.title: AMR chatbot could prevent drug-resistant infections in African hospitals
News.content:
A phone-based chatbot advising medics how to prescribe antibiotics has helped raise the quality of care in African hospitals and should stop bugs developing dangerous resistance, developers say.

Staff at four hospitals across Zambia and Kenya have been using two digital tools in a pilot project to try to address one of the world’s biggest health threats.

Anti-microbial resistance (AMR) is caused by germs evolving so that medicines such as antibiotics designed to kill them no longer work.

The menace is linked to nearly five million deaths each year and makes it increasingly difficult to treat infections. The annual death toll could nearly double in the next 25 years, according to some forecasts.

The rise in AMR is being significantly driven by the misuse and overuse of antimicrobials in human medicine and in agriculture.

Using antibiotics when they are not necessary, using the wrong ones, or getting the dosage wrong, all add to the chances that bugs will develop resistance.

With a shortage of new drugs in the development pipeline, one push to defeat AMR has been to get medics to stick to existing prescription, dosage and treatment advice.

The Antibiotic Stewardship Programme through Innovation, Research, and Education (ASPIRE) is trying to give them guidance using technology they already have in their pockets.

News.title: Tottenham new boys score in shoot-out win over Sydney FC
News.content:
Tonali was brought on as a half-time substitute, before Robertson took the captain’s armband from Archie Gray after he was introduced in the 65th minute.

The former Liverpool left-back delivered three dangerous crosses which went unconverted, something of a theme for a Spurs team who failed to make the most of long spells of dominance.

James Maddison and Mateus Fernandes were not in the match-day squad, while Pedro Porro, Marcos Senesi, Cristian Romero, Micky van de Ven and Jean Paul van Hecke have yet to join the group after the World Cup.

There was another impressive showing from 17-year-old prospect Luca Williams-Barnett, who is pushing for first-team opportunities this upcoming season.

Penalties followed the final whistle, with Spurs scoring all four of their spot kicks. Goalkeeper Martin Dubravka, signed on a free transfer this summer, saved one and Sydney FC’s Josh Lacey hit the post to give Spurs the spoils 4-2.

News.title: Recovery aids and building muscle: Welsh weightlifter Laura Hughes answers your questions
News.content:
Laura Hughes first discovered weightlifting while training at her local Crossfit gym, making the transition from amateur gym-goer to competitive lifting.

Now a member of the Welsh national weightlifting squad, the 33-year-old holds the Welsh record for both the snatch and the clean and jerk (the two official competitive lifts in weightlifting) and is currently third overall in the women’s Welsh rankings. Hughes won bronze at this year’s Commonwealth Games in Glasgow, following on from her third place at the 2018 Games in Australia.

We caught up with her for our Readers Ask series, where industry specialists answer questions from our Telegraph Recommended Reader Panel.

Who inspired you to get into weightlifting?

Olamilekan, South East

Originally, it was lots of different people, particularly general gym goers who were doing weightlifting at my gym. As I’ve grown as an athlete and become more competitive, I’ve had other inspirations.

Most notably, coming into [the Commonwealth Games], it has to be Gareth [Evans], our coach. Looking back at his performance in 2018 when he won his gold medal is so inspiring. [English lifter] Emily Godley was another competitor in 2018. She won the gold medal in my category and I just remember thinking that she was on fire that day.

What are the best exercises for you to build muscle mass?

Norman, Wales

We spend a lot of time doing our main lifts, so snatches, clean and jerks, but we also do lots of pulls and squats. I spend a lot of time doing accessory work to make sure that my body stays healthy, especially being an older athlete. I’ve put on quite a lot of muscle in this last block just from going heavier and pushing my limits with my main lifts.

What advice would you give to people who want to improve their strength?

David, North West

The most important thing is consistency. As long as you’re doing something, do it regularly, even if it’s twice a week. Don’t be afraid of picking up some dumbbells. If you’ve got somebody that can teach you how to lift weights properly, that’s going to be the best option. Do it safely, do it consistently, and don’t be afraid to try new strength exercises.

News.title: Explosive mpox outbreak causes 3,000 cases in Madagascar
News.content:
More than 3,000 cases of mpox have been recorded in Madagascar after the virus spread from a single port city to some of the country’s busiest coastal hubs.

A total of 3,022 cases and 20 deaths have been recorded as of this week, with cases in Toamasina and Taolagnaro accounting for more than half of all diagnoses.

The outbreak has been linked to Clade 1b mpox, a strain that emerged in the Democratic Republic of the Congo in 2024, prompting the World Health Organization (WHO) to declare a global public health emergency at the time.

“The main factor driving the continued spread of the disease is human mobility, seeding new outbreaks in areas where the virus has not circulated before,” Professor Carlos Maluquer de Motes of the University of Surrey told The Telegraph.

“Under-reporting is likely, with the real number of cases exceeding what is being reported.”

News.title: Chelsea in 10-goal thriller as ‘Alonso ball’ brings risk and reward
News.content:
Chelsea’s first match under the management of Xabi Alonso was a 10-goal thriller in Australia, as the Premier League side eventually showed their class in a 6-4 win over Western Sydney Wanderers.

Star striker João Pedro, who was controversially left out of Brazil’s World Cup squad, scored a nine-minute hat-trick after coming off the bench with half an hour of the friendly remaining.

Alonso had selected a youthful team for the first hour before bringing nine senior players, including João Pedro, into the side in the second half. According to Transfermarkt, Chelsea’s squad is valued at over £1.3bn while their opponents a more modest £5.86m.

Teenage signing Dastan Satpayev, midfielder Dario Essugo and winger Jamie Gittens also found the net for Chelsea, who were defensively vulnerable for long spells for the game.

Here are five things Telegraph Sport learned from Alonso’s first match.

João Pedro picks up where he left off

João Pedro scored 13 goals in the second half of last season and his impressive performances resulted in the 24-year-old being named Chelsea’s player of the campaign. It was something of a surprise, then, when he was left out of Carlo Ancelotti’s Brazil squad this summer.

The good news for Chelsea is that João Pedro’s absence from the World Cup has given him plenty of time to recover ahead of the new campaign, and he looked thrillingly sharp in his second-half performance against Western Sydney Wanderers. The difference in class between João Pedro and Liam Delap, the man he replaced, was clear for all to see.

Two of the Brazilian’s three goals were classy, composed finishes — and he also created a goal for Gittens after surging past three defenders on the left wing. João Pedro looks like he means business.

Sports.title: Man Utd ‘discuss Igor Thiago transfer’ with Red Devils looking to add competition for Benjamin Sesko
Sports.content:
MANCHESTER UNITED are keeping tabs on Brentford star Igor Thiago as they look to add significant firepower to their frontline, reports suggest.

Jacobs revealed the Red Devils are weighing up a swoop for Thiago, 25, after a stunning campaign that saw him finishing as the Premier League’s second top scorer.

Sports.title: Jadon Sancho training next to Man Utd HQ at ground of 10th tier minnows who are coached by Reds’ icon’s brother
Sports.content:
JADON SANCHO has been training at 10th tier minnows Flixton FC – just a stone’s throw away from Manchester United’s training ground.

Sancho is now a free agent after his Old Trafford nightmare officially ended this summer, calling time on years of endless loan spells.



The 26-year-old winger, whom United splashed £73m on in 2021, has been using upgraded non-league facilities at Flixton’s 2,000-capacity Valley Road ground.

In a club interview, Sancho said: “You’ve got a nice layout here. It’s the first time I’ve seen a nice pitch [in this area] apart from United and City.”



Flixton are gearing up for their first competitive season since going bust in 2012, having been brought back from the dead by a new investor last year.

United legend Ryan Giggs‘ estranged brother Rhodri Giggs, who previously managed Salford City, was appointed as assistant manager last summer.



The cash investment in the facilities comes after American financier Christopher Garcia, CEO of US based Wilshire Quinn Capital, purchased the club in February 2025.

Originally opened by Sir Alex Ferguson back in 1995, Flixton’s Valley Road ground had been reduced to hosting Sunday League games before being slapped with a £500,000 price tag on Rightmove in January 2025.

While weighing up his next options, Sancho promised he’d be in the stands to watch Flixton play next Tuesday, just a ten-minute drive away from Carrington.

The London-born forward has drawn interest from Qatari club Al Rayyan and has been previously targeted by Roma in Serie A.

Sports.title: Who is Matthias Jaissle? Newcastle set to appoint little-known Al Ahli boss as Eddie Howe’s replacement
Sports.content:
NEWCASTLE are expected to name little-known Matthias Jaissle as their new head coach after Eddie Howe’s shock departure.

News of Howe‘s exit – just weeks before the start of the new Premier League season – has rocked fans on Tyneside.



The 48-year-old ends his five-year tenure as one of Newcastle‘s most successful managers after guiding the club to their first major trophy in 70 years by winning the Carabao Cup in 2025.

He also led the Magpies to Champions League qualification in 2023 and 2025.



It’s understood Howe‘s departure comes after he told Toon chiefs he wants to take a break from coaching.

Newcastle are now poised to name their replacement, with Jaissle expected to take the St James’ Park hotseat – SunSport brings you the lowdown on the young coach.

Who is potential new Newcastle boss Matthias Jaissle?

Jaissle, 38, is currently in charge of Saudi Pro League side Al Ahli, who, like Newcastle, are majority-owned by Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund (PIF).

The German was a talented centre-back in his playing days, but was forced to retire in 2014 at the age of just 26 after never truly recovering from a knee injury picked up five years earlier.

Former Manchester United boss Ralph Rangnick came to Jaissle’s aid after that and invited him on a trainee programme with RB Leipzig’s youth academy.



The pair knew each other as Rangnick coached a young Jaissle during his time as manager of Hoffenheim and he reached out in his new role as RB Leipzig’s head of sport.

He temporarily left the Austrian giants in 2021, becoming a head coach for the first time at Liefering.

In his first season, the German led the team to second in the Austrian second tier, the club’s joint best-ever finish.

Jaissle’s exploits earned him the top job at RB Salzburg, replacing Jesse Marsch.

During his time in charge at the Red Bull Arena, he managed the likes of Benjamin Sesko and Karim Adeyemi, who now play for Manchester United and Barcelona respectively.



He won the Austrian Bundesliga in both of his two seasons in charge and was heralded as one of the brightest young coaches in Europe.

In 2023, Jaissle joined Al Ahli, where he has won the Asian Champions League Elite twice and the Saudi Super Cup.

The Saudi club have England striker Ivan Toney and former Chelsea goalkeeper Edouard Mendy on their books.

Three Lions boss Thomas Tuchel was a youth coach at Stuttgart when Jaissle was coming through as a player and the two Germans spoke before Toney was included in England’s World Cup squad this summer.

At the time of the squad announcement, Tuchel said: “I had fantastic feedback from his club coach, who was my player and I have a close connection with him.”



What is Jaissle’s style of play?

Newcastle fans will be happy to know Jaissle likes to play high-pressing attacking football, not too dissimilar to what we have seen from Howe’s sides in the past.

During his time at Al Ahli, the German has often played a 4-2-3-1, but Jaissle has previously explained it’s more about principles of play than the formation.

Speaking to Sky Sports, he said: “It is not about formations that much. It is more how you want to play, how you want to attack, how you want to defend.

“If you understand that and the players understand that, tactically you are much more flexible and the formation is not that important.”

“It can be demanding for players. These days the players are more and more involved in tactical things.



“Every coach and every club works with principles, so every player has to know a lot of things, tactically, in each phase of the game. I think that’s a big change.”

In 2024, Jaissle drew upon some of the coaches who have influenced his career, but he insisted he has his own style.

The German told GiveMeSport: “I have always tried to be authentic as a coach and find my own way.

“Of course, I have influences. Ralf Rangnick played a big part in developing my ideas because I played under him for most of my playing career.

“And in my youth, I had Thomas Tuchel, so I have followed his principles and career. Then there’s Jurgen Klopp – I often looked at the transitions he put in place with Liverpool.



“In possession, I like how Pep Guardiola finds structure and balance. And there’s a lot to take from Roberto De Zerbi’s build-up as well. It’s a constant learning process.

“I am always refining my style, but essentially, and I know it’s easy to say, we want dominance in all phases of the game.

“It’s a never-ending process because you always need to develop your ideas as a coach without abandoning your roots.

“At Salzburg, I played a 4-4-2 with a diamond midfield. At Al-Ahli, we use a 4-2-3-1 system. You have to adjust to the squad you have as well as the circumstances.”

Sports.title: Eddie Howe’s exit shows Newcastle may never compete at top of Premier League, the owners’ 2030 title dream is impossible
Sports.content:
WHEN Eddie Howe agreed to take the reins at stricken Newcastle United nearly five years ago, he did not do so with the aim of treading water.

He had a vision, backed by the new Saudi money after the miserable years under Mike Ashley, and he was raring to go having taken a year out of the game.



We sat together in a hotel from where you could see across to St. James’ Park in the Tyneside night and Howe’s eyes lit up at the sight of the cathedral on the hill.

This was where he was meant to be, this was the big job he had always wanted.



For over an hour we chewed the fat and I left in no doubt that this man would spend every waking minute to try and make Newcastle great.

Not for a moment could that total commitment ever be questioned.



He also delivered us a first domestic trophy for 70 years and no Newcastle fan will ever forget the date, March 16, 2025, when we put Liverpool to the sword at Wembley.

But this is a man who knew he was spent.

Howe did not have a hope of delivering on the hierarchy’s brief to bag the Premier League title by 2030, especially when the best players were being sold and replaced by untested youngsters.

He had given it a go and given us some memorable Champions League nights too but, no matter how rich the club’s owners are, financial restrictions mean it will be years before Newcastle can compete right at the top, if ever.



BEST FREE BETS AND BETTING SIGN UP OFFERS

As when he decided to leave Bournemouth, a team he’d transformed, Howe realised his part in the project was over.

Friends say he has gone with sadness and a somewhat flat feeling ahead of the new season but that there is no ill-will towards the club.

Howe told them he was ready to go and they were free to replace him. He was also aware they had got a new man in place, he just didn’t know it was going to be confirmed this morning.

Howe doesn’t know what he will do next but he needs a break.



Whenever he goes back to St. James’, either as a guest or as boss of a new club, he can be guaranteed a rapturous reception from all four corners of the ground.

Sports.title: Quarter of sports fans believe they could score a goal in a Premier League match, new poll finds
Sports.content:
A QUARTER of sports fans reckon they could score a goal in a Premier League match, while one in 10 claim they could last a round in the ring with a pro boxer.

The study of 2,000 adults who enjoy watching sport found many think they could hold their own against some of the best athletes in the world.



One in seven (14 per cent) think they could be on a par with a professional golfer over one hole, while 22 per cent are confident they could beat them in crazy golf, and 18 per cent reckon they would be able to return a serve from a top tennis player.

While 14 per cent even think they could manage a lap of a Formula 1 track against the top drivers without coming last.



It also emerged 14 per cent think they could finish a stage of the Tour de France without embarrassing themselves against the competition.

The study was commissioned by Staysure, ahead of the Legends golf tour sponsored by the brand, which gets underway next week at Trump International Golf Links, and gives amateurs the unique opportunity to play alongside the pros in its Pro-Am event.

Corin Rogerson, director of sponsorship for the insurer, said: “Pro sport isn’t as easy as people seemingly think it could be, but these findings show just how confident many fans are when watching from the sofa or the stands.

“It can seem easy when spectating, but in reality, elite athletes dedicate years to perfecting their craft, building the physical fitness, mental resilience and technical skill needed to compete at the very top.

“It is easy to underestimate just how difficult these sports are until you are faced with the speed, pressure and precision involved.

“That is what makes watching the professionals do what they do so impressive.”



But the research found reality clearly does not hold people back, as 57 per cent reckon there are some adults who think they could compete with a professional athlete.

While 66 per cent of those put this down to some simply over-estimating their own abilities, 59 per cent believe it’s due to the sports looking easier than they are.

More than half (56 per cent) also think it’s due to people undervaluing just how skilled the sportspeople really are.

With 80 per cent believing that watching professional sport can make people become ‘armchair experts’ who underestimate how difficult it is to play at that level.

When it comes to golf in particular, 38 per cent think an amateur would have a chance against a professional, believing it can all come down to one lucky shot (52 per cent), and because pros make mistakes too (51 per cent).



The research, carried out, via OnePoll, found 82 per cent find stories of amateurs and underdogs triumphing in sport inspiring, and 42 per cent would be keen to watch a novice take on a pro golfer in a head-to-head challenge.

Corin Rogerson for Staysure added: “As a nation, many of us are clearly willing to back ourselves when it comes to taking on the professionals, whether that is stepping onto a golf course, returning a serve, or lasting in the ring.

“It was a fun reminder of the confidence many sports fans have.”

Sports.title: Uefa statement in full as Gianni Infantino blasted for ‘governance by intimidation’ over shameless World Cup plan
Sports.content:
UEFA have “unanimously and unequivocally” slammed Fifa’s controversial World Cup plans and accused them of intimidation tactics.

The Fifa president’s controversial proposal involves transferring control of top tournaments like the World Cup to a new subsidiary, followed by the sale of a substantial portion of the business.



European football’s governing body has led the backlash against the plot and hosted a virtual meeting with its 55 member associations today.

And Uefa president Aleksander Ceferin has blasted Gianni Infantino for his plans amid the Uefa-Fifa civil war.



Uefa has since published a statement that reads: “UEFA and its national associations will not participate in Fifa competitions.

“UEFA and its 55 member associations stand as one.



“We unanimously and unequivocally reject Fifa’s proposal to transfer ownership interests in the World Cup and other Fifa competitions to private investors.

“The World Cup cannot be treated as an investment product. It is one of football’s greatest sporting legacies.

“It has been built over generations by players, national teams and supporters across every continent.

“No part of it should ever be surrendered to private investors. The World Cup is not for sale.

“It is both irresponsible and indefensible that a proposal of such significance for football was conceived in secret and brought to the brink of approval without any meaningful consultation with those entrusted with stewarding the game.

“This is not merely a profound failure of leadership, but an abdication of Fifa’s duty as the custodian of world football.

“National associations around the world are now presented with an ultimatum: accept the irreversible capture of football’s greatest competitions or bear the consequences.

“This is not a ‘democratic decision’, but governance by intimidation – an act of coercion unworthy of an institution entrusted with the stewardship of the global game.

“But our opposition goes far beyond process.



“The moment external investors acquire ownership interests in Fifa competitions, football changes forever.

“Commercial return becomes a permanent obligation. Investor expectations become a daily pressure.

“From that moment onwards, every decision on the international calendar, every decision on competition formats and every decision shaping the future of football is no longer driven by what best serves the game, but by what best serves shareholders.



“This model has no place in world football. Football’s future cannot be dictated by the expectations of those whose first duty is to maximise financial return.

“Nor can the interests of national associations, leagues, clubs, players and supporters become subordinate to investor returns.

“Football cannot mortgage its future for financial gain.

“Europe’s position is clear. We will never lend this model our legitimacy.

“No one has the moral authority to sell what they merely hold in trust for the next generation.



“As a result of today’s discussion, no UEFA national teams will participate in any FIFA competition for so long as these proposals remain alive.

“Unless this proposal has been abandoned in its entirety and binding assurances have been given that Fifa will never again open its governance or competitions to private ownership.

“Nobody should be in any doubt: UEFA and its national associations will oppose these plans with absolute determination.

“There are moments when institutions are judged not by what they are prepared to accept, but by what they refuse to compromise.

Sports.title: Premier League stars face at least 10-MATCH bans for ‘aggravated breaches’ as FA impose new punishment
Sports.content:
CRACKDOWN Premier League stars face at least 10-MATCH bans for ‘aggravated breaches’ as FA impose new punishment

Credit: Not known, clear with picture desk

FOOTBALLERS will now be hit with a whopping 10-MATCH ban as standard if they commit an aggravated breach of FA rules.

The new sanction guidelines have been introduced ahead of the 2026/27 season as part of a firmer stance against discriminatory conduct.



An aggravated breach is defined in FA Rule E3.2 as “any misconduct that includes an express or implied reference to any one or more of the following characteristics: ethnic origin, colour, race, nationality, religion or belief, sex, gender, gender reassignment, sexual orientation, or disability“.

Recent sanction guidelines have recommended bans of between six and 12 matches to the independent regulatory commissions who dish out the punishments.



But now a standard suspension will be at least 10 matches, the FA has confirmed.

They wrote on their website: “We are committed to delivering a game free from discrimination.



“While significant progress has been made in recent years, discriminatory conduct continues to be a challenge across the game.

“Enhanced measures are necessary to tackle this abhorrent conduct, and our updated sanction guidelines will now require Regulatory Commissions to impose a standard suspension of at least 10 matches in these circumstances.”

Aggravating factors would allow commissions to impose a ban higher than 10 matches, with mitigating factors permitting them to lower it to a minimum of six matches.

Players could be slapped with bans in excess of 12 matches – or a time-based suspension – if they are charged despite already having an aggravated breach on their record.



Fulham‘s Chris Donnell was banned for six matches last year for using abusive and/or insulting words with a reference to disability.

That punishment could be heightened under the new guidelines, unless mitigating factors were presented to the commission.

Tranmere’s Sam Finlay was slapped with a 13-game ban last year for using a homophobic slur.

And Preston’s Milutin Osmajic was banned for nine matches in November after racially abusing Hannibal Mejbri.

Sports.title: Chelsea, Sunderland and Nottingham Forest caught out as Premier League gambling ban bites
Sports.content:
Three Premier League teams are poised to start the 2026/27 season without front-of-shirt sponsors after falling to navigate the market in the wake of a ban on gambling companies.

It was way back in April 2023 when Premier League clubs agreed to get rid of gambling companies on the front of their shirts. And yet Chelsea, Sunderland and Nottingham Forest have so far been unable to find a suitable replacement.

Obscure gambling companies had become part of the furniture of elite football, delighted to pay millions to for brand exposure - often in markets where gambling is illegal. Premier League sides were more than happy to accept their money - often worth double the offers from non-gambling companies - despite ethical concerns.

After mounting pressure, including from the government, that came to an end this summer. Eleven of the 20 teams in the Premier League last season had a gambling company emblazoned on their shirt. Three of those were relegated, leaving eight teams that needed to find a replacement this summer.

‌

England and UEFA nations WILL BOYCOTT World Cup in protest over Gianni Infantino sale plan READ MORE :

Six have been successful, but alongside Chelsea - who have had their own sponsor struggles in recent years - Sunderland and Forest look set to go sponsor-less 22 days before the season kicks off. Inside the commercial teams of Premier League clubs, gambling sponsors had been viewed as too good to turn down. They paid more than other companies and wanted less in return, acting as a simple billboard to millions of viewers.

While Aston Villa, Bournemouth, Brentford, Crystal Palace, Everton and Fulham managed to secure new sponsors, likely on reduced rates, Sunderland and Forest have held out. Sean Connell, editor of The Sponsor, an independent sponsorship research and valuation publication, believes they have become victim of " the most competitive and difficult sponsorship environment" in Premier League history. In short, commercial teams have been forced to do more work for less reward.

"It’s an incredibly competitive sponsorship market," he tells Mirror Football. "The number of brands willing to put their hands in their pocket and stump up £5m to £15m to sponsor a Premier League club is already significantly reduced due to factors outside the sports landscape.

‌



View 4 Images Sunderland have gone from gambling company W88 to no sponsor (Image: Johnnie Izquierdo/Getty Images)

"Sponsors are under incredible amount of scrutiny to justify their expenditure. Then there's an unusually high number of teams in the market looking for a sponsor – in a normal year it might only be one or two, but it was 11 this summer.

"The gambling ban has taken what was already a shrinking pool of sponsors and removed a healthy chunk of those. It’s created what I believe is the most competitive and difficult sponsorship environment that Premier League clubs have ever faced."

The gambling ban has been looming for over three years and Connell believes some have been guilty of failing to burying their heads in the sand. Mirror Football contacted Chelsea, Sunderland and Nottingham Forest to request comment.

‌



Premier League front-of-shirt sponsors 2026/27 Arsenal – Emirates (Airline) Aston Villa – Visit Rwanda (Tourism) Bournemouth – Vitality (Insurance) Brentford – Indeed (Employment) Brighton – American Express (Bank) Chelsea – NONE Coventry – Monzo (Bank) Crystal Palace – Temporal (Software platform) Everton – CMC Markets (Financial services) Fulham – ClickHouse (Technology) Hull City – Corendon Airlines (Airline) Ipswich – Halo (Software) Leeds – Red Bull (Drinks) Liverpool – Standard Chartered (Bank) Manchester City – Etihad Airways (Airline) Manchester United – Snapdragon (Electronics) Newcastle – Knox (Sports drinks) Nottingham Forest – NONE (previously Bally’s) Sunderland – NONE (previously W88) Tottenham – AIA (Insurance)

“The profits and revenue have been so much greater than they would have been that nobody has taken any meaningful strides to address this," Connell says. "They have continued to take the money while the sun shone. Now some like Forest and Sunderland are in a difficult position.

“I think the clubs have been waiting to see what the highest possible deal is at the last possible moment. For some clubs that strategy worked out, for others like Sunderland and Forest they have presumably determined that the value of the deal on the table is not adequate and that holding out rather than underselling is the best strategy.”

Chelsea's situation is different. Remarkably, the Blues have not had a permanent front‑of‑shirt sponsor since their deal with Three ended in 2023. In February they announced a front-of-shirt deal until the end of the season with AI technology company IFS, but are now once again sponsor-less.

‌



View 4 Images Nottingham Forest have been unable to replace their gambling sponsor (Image: Gualter Fatia/Getty Images)

It has been reported that Chelsea have been holding out for £65m per season for their front-of-shirt sponsorship. Yet their 10th-place finish, and failure to secure any European football next season, appears to have damaged their chances.

While the gambling ban has undoubtedly impacted the revenues of Premier League clubs, particularly those outside the elite, who have more pulling power, it is a landmark moment in the league. R esearch in 2023 found that betting logos appear up to 3,500 times during TV games, a troubling reality for vulnerable people and gambling addicts.

Will Prochaska, director of the Coalition to End Gambling Ads (CEGA), said: “Andy Burnham has said we should 'relegate gambling sponsorship of sport to the history books' and we agree.

‌



View 4 Images Gambling sponsors had been ubiquitous in the Premier League (Image: Mark Fletcher/Getty Images)

“Fans will have little sympathy with clubs struggling to replace front-of-shirt gambling sponsors, and there's more than enough money in the game to ensure football can thrive without gambling revenues.

“Formula 1 cried foul that ending tobacco sponsorship would destroy the sport, but it's gone from strength to strength. Ridding football of its links to the gambling sector is an opportunity to turn a corner, not a burden.”

While gambling companies are still allowed on the sleeves of shirts in the Premier League, the gambling gold rush, when millions flowed into the game from obscure gambling entities operating via “white label” agreements with a company in the Isle of Man, are over. The results will be obvious come the first weekend of the season.

‌

Sports.title: 'No Plan B': Will Matthias Jaissle have tactical flexibility Eddie Howe never showed at Newcastle?
Sports.content:
Eddie Howe has left his role as Newcastle United manager, bringing to a close a hugely successful five-year spell in which the former Bournemouth boss took the Magpies back into the Champions League and ended a 56-year wait for a trophy by beating Liverpool in the EFL Cup final.

However, Howe increasingly faced criticism for not developing a successful 'Plan B' to his brand of high-intensity, physical football, which saw results suffer when fatigue, the demand of European football, and injuries impacted his first-choice team.

AI 'supercomputer' Machine Football's analysis of the manager widely expected to take over from Howe, current Al Ahli boss Matthias Jaissle, shows how his style of play has evolved over time and could be just what Newcastle need to once again instil a clear identity.

Eddie Howe told what made his Newcastle job 'unsustainable' before sudden departure READ MORE :

How Jaissle's style has evolved

2023/24:

‌



Jaissle's first Al Ahli side were what Machine Football categorises as 'high-octane pressers', setting up for the majority of games in a 4-2-3-1 formation and relying heavily on dribbling and forward carries alongside an aggressive press.

That approach delivered 1.85 points per game and continental qualification. But Jaissle did not stop there, evolving his side further ahead of the following season.

2024/25:

Al Ahli developed into what Machine Football categorises as 'aggressive disruptors', with the emphasis shifting away from wing play and towards creating higher-quality chances with expected goals rising from 1.59 per 90 to 1.97 and points per game increasing to 2.04.

‌



Your Machine Football glossary of football tactics, data and stats buzzwords READ MORE :

2025/26:

Next, Jaissle added flexibility without changing the identity. Alongside the primary 4-2-3-1 setup - which he used in more than 40% of games - the German introduced a 4-3-3 variation in 22% of his games and, in roughly one match out of every five, more of a low-block counter style of play built on a traditional 4-4-2.

While the formations may have varied, the approach didn't. Al Ahli's PPDA (presses per defensive action - a pressing measurement where the lower the score, the more aggressive the press) was a high-octane 9.02.

Al Ahli also averaged 7.18 through passes per game – well above the Saudi Pro League average of 4.13 – and 19.83 touches inside the opposition box, comfortably ahead of the league average of 16.46.

‌



Rather than dominating possession, Al Ahli look to win the ball high and attack quickly. That approach resulted in Jaissle's best domestic season yet, averaging 2.38 points per game while winning a second consecutive AFC Champions League Elite title.

View 4 Images Cohesion: Newcastle v Al Ahli (2025/26). Al Ahli's weaker connections between defensive and midfield lines reflects their preference for vertical passes rather than slow build-up (Image: Machine Football)

Howe's 'flip-flopping' tactical approach

Who Jaissle is tactically suggests a significant change from the Newcastle side he looks set to inherit. The contrast becomes clearer when the numbers are put side by side.

The perception that Howe never managed to successfully implement a 'Plan B' comes from a run of seasons where the club's fortunes flip-flopped. Newcastle's style clearly changed from season to season during his tenure at St James' Park, but results also yo-yo'd.

‌



In 2022/23 Newcastle were what Machine Football's analysis classes as 'high-octane pressers' and enjoyed their best-ever points return (2.09 PPG).

The 2023/24 season, however, saw Champions League group stage football return and a shift towards a 'passive controllers' model accompany it.

In practice, Newcastle were playing more patient, lower-tempo football focused on control. It was still productive (1.72 PPG) but represented a step down in intensity and earned only a seventh placed Premier League finish.

In 2024/25 - no European football again - Howe swung back toward a more progressive, 'attacking engine' playing style. This helped their PPG bounce back up to 1.81 resulting in fifth place and Champions League qualification for a second time under Howe.

‌



Another flip then followed in 2025-26 as they moved into 'possession builders' - the most control-oriented identity of the four seasons - but only in just over half of their games, as PPG (1.26) reached its lowest ebb of any of Howe's four full seasons and Newcastle stuttered to 12th place in the league.

What this topsy-turvy playing identity suggests is that the new manager's style could help the Magpies get back to something like the best version of themselves from 22/23.

View 4 Images Stats comparison of Newcastle and Al Ahli 2025/26: Note how despite taking fewer shots, Al Ahli had a higher percentage of their efforts hit the target and a higher xG per 90 (Image: Machine Football)

Taking the stats from 2025-26, Newcastle and Al Ahli's possession is almost identical, but everything that follows is different. Last season, Al Ahli completed around 80 fewer passes per game - yet attempted more than twice as many through balls, created higher-quality chances and conceded almost half as many goals.

‌



Jaissle's style, then, is built entirely around progressing the ball quickly and attacking before opponents can reset.

Eddie Howe was FAILED by Newcastle United owners - he should have walked away earlier READ MORE :

Alan Shearer shares honest take on Eddie Howe’s Newcastle exit and selling best players READ MORE :

Premier League rival and six other clubs Eddie Howe could join after shock Newcastle United exit READ MORE :

Can Saudi success translate to Premier League?

While the change in approach might seem drastic, it looks set to get the Gallowgate End on its feet and - most importantly - the underlying numbers suggest it could translate into results, albeit with star players continuing to depart Newcastle.

Across 34 Saudi Pro League matches, Al Ahli scored 71 goals (2.09 per game), conceded just 25 (0.74 per game), kept 17 clean sheets and won 73.5% of their league matches.

Their expected goals total (66.73) closely mirrored their actual return, suggesting the attacking output is sustainable rather than the product of an unusually clinical season.

‌



View 4 Images A possible best XI for Jaissle's Newcastle based on the current options available (Image: Machine Football)

Newcastle's numbers tell a different story. They scored 53 goals in 38 Premier League games (1.39 per game), won just 36.8% of their matches and finished with expected goals for and against that were almost identical (59.23 xG versus 59.5 xGA).

The difference isn't how much of the ball the two teams have. It's what they do with it. Now all that's left is for Jaissle to prove he can make the same principles work in the Premier League.

‌
