VAD telehealth endorsed at ALP conference A Labor push to lift the ban on accessing voluntary assisted dying through telehealth has triggered a warning about unintended consequences for vulnerable Australians.

There may be efforts from some in government to persuade Chaney to hold off from acting on Tuesday week, with suggestions that a softly, softly approach might get better results. Chaney's present inclination is to strike while the iron's hot.

But Albanese has indicated not just his personal view but that he wants to keep tight control of the issue.

"I'm a supporter of voluntary euthanasia," he told the ABC at the weekend.

"But it's also important that protections be placed around it. Now, if someone has a heart attack or an acute health condition, they need a doctor, they can't do that over telehealth, and I think that someone ending their life […] should be face-to-face recognition and face-to-face engagement". Removing this ban would undermine support for VAD, he suggested.

Pressed on whether he would allow a vote in parliament, Albanese said: "What I will allow is for colleagues to express a view. […] It's up to the cabinet to decide […] and cabinet makes decisions after and in consultation with the caucus."

Those who have spoken to him in the past about the issue say he is very forceful in his view. He is said to believe telehealth could weaken the safeguards around VAD.

Why we have the ban

The ban on the use of a carriage service to transmit suicide-related messaging dates back far before the inception of telehealth. It was inserted when the criminal code was amended in reaction to the internet and suicide-related material.

Then Liberal attorney-general Philip Ruddock told parliament in 2005: "The bill seeks to protect vulnerable individuals […] but does not seek to stifle legitimate debate on euthanasia or suicide-related issues.

ABC Politics in your inbox Sign up to the ABC Politics newsletter with Courtney Gould

"These provisions make it clear that the offences only apply where the person intends to use the material concerned to counsel or incite suicide, or to promote or provide instruction on a method of committing suicide."

A 2023 federal court decision ruled that VAD came under the definition of suicide, and so a telehealth consultation would contravene the law.

When the Albanese government granted the territories the right to legislate for VAD — removing the prohibition imposed under the Howard government in 1997 — Albanese was against changing the criminal law provision.

Loading

Ministers on each side

How the cabinet divides on the issue will be significant. Apart from Albanese and Rowland, Burke would presumably be against change — his political opposition to euthanasia goes back to when he worked closely with then Liberal MP the late Kevin Andrews to overturn the Northern Territory assisted dying law. Burke, not in federal parliament then, was executive director of Euthanasia No!.

But on the other side of the argument is a weighty voice — that of Health Minister Mark Butler. Butler reportedly was influential in getting the issue debated at the Labor conference, part of a trade off for the left going soft on other contentious matters.

Asked by The Conversation on Thursday about the conference decision and future action, Butler stuck to the formal dictum: "The national platform and resolutions of the party, represent short and long-term aspirations of the ALP. The government of the day sets government policies."

In the Senate, the Greens' Sarah Hanson-Young will bring a private senator's bill forward in the first sitting fortnight of the coming session. "We could have this law fixed by the end of the year if there is willingness across all sides of the parliament to work together."

But in government circles, advocates say there's a long way to go, suggesting more would need to be done on clinical safeguards. And that's assuming Albanese could eventually be got across the line.

Michelle Grattan is a professorial fellow at the University of Canberra and chief political correspondent at The Conversation, where this article first appeared.

World.title: Ease of chargebacks crippling small businesses as banks fail to take responsibility
World.content:
If it walks like a duck and quacks like a duck, the famous proverb states the wild bird is, in fact, most likely a duck.

Taking the duck at face value seems to be enough evidence for the majority that it has become a well-known idiom.

What about a financial dispute? Most would agree that face value wouldn't suffice when it comes to evidence.

Instead, written proof, documentation, or even photos create a much stronger case.

But what happens when even this isn't enough?

Small businesses across the country have fallen victim to a modern type of fraud known as chargebacks, leaving them frustrated at the lack of support from bank and financially stressed as they lose the product, the money, and are then hit with a fine.

To give you an example of what a fraudulent chargeback looks like, it's where a customer purchases a product online, but once it arrives, they claim it never did or that it wasn't them who bought it, lodging a chargeback with their bank to get the money back.

The business owner then has an opportunity to dispute.

For some, the evidence is poor — the customer's word against the small business owners, with the customer almost always coming out on top.

'Friendly fraud' costing retailers thousands Retailers are grappling with an online version of shoplifting and are calling for better protections.

But some business owners are providing serious evidence that a customer did receive their product, and still, it isn't enough.

Take Alex, for example, who runs a small homeware business. In February this year, one of his customers admitted in writing the chargeback dispute he lodged was a mistake.

"The card that this was charged to was the cause of the error. It is a debit card that belongs to my son," the customer said in an email.

Alex then sent this email correspondence to NAB, as evidence for the chargeback dispute.

A month later, NAB denied Alex's dispute on the grounds it had "reviewed compelling evidence" and that "the customer continues to dispute the transaction", leaving him out of pocket, without the product, and paying a fine.

In the end, the customer sent him the money via bank transfer.

No protections under framework

This kind of admission would likely stack up in a court of law, so why didn't it when presented to a bank?

Nina Kutzner talks chargebacks at the recent Online Retailer Conference in Sydney. (ABC News: Adelaide Miller)

At an Online Retailer Conference in Sydney last week, Nina Kutzner, founder of the Payment Dispute Institute, said under the current regulatory framework, there were virtually no protections granted to business owners when it came to how a dispute was investigated.

"None of these documents are talking about this needs to be fair to retailers," she said.

" In order to achieve fairer outcomes, we need to uplift frameworks given the tone has changed. "

Ms Kutzner worked across several major banks as well as payment schemes before creating the Payment Dispute Institute (PDI).

Nina Kutzner says more protections are needed for small businesses. (Supplied: Nina Kutzner)

PDI is an independent research, analysis, and advocacy organisation dedicated to payment disputes and chargeback frameworks, where Ms Kutzner is paid through private consultation work with merchants.

Despite online payments advancing rapidly, the chargeback dispute mechanism hasn't been updated for decades.

Instead, those looking for answers about who holds responsibility in this space waste time as they are handballed over to the next institution.

It's a hot potato

The financial regulator ASIC does not legislate card schemes, which include chargeback frameworks and responsibilities.

The recent Online Retailer Conference at the ICC in Sydney. (ABC News: Adelaide Miller)

That responsibility lies with the international card schemes, which include Visa and Mastercard.

But both say they only provide "infrastructure and rules that underpin chargebacks" and it's the responsibility of the issuing banks to decide outcomes.

As for a bank ignoring compelling evidence, Ms Kutzner said it came down to two reasons: loyalty to their customer, and the risk of a financial penalty.

"If a customer is not satisfied with the disputes process, they can go to AFCA [Australian Financial Complaints Authority] … however, a merchant doesn't have the same pathway, it can't go to AFCA," she said.

Loading...

AFCA can then hit the bank with a fine if it sees fit.

"It's one-sided policing only. Naturally, it's cheaper to side with a consumer over a business," Ms Kutzner said.

According to the Australian Bureau of Statistics, chargeback decisions favour the customer, with 72 per cent who claim card fraud fully reimbursed by their card issuer in 2023–24, totalling $477 million.

Worldwide, chargebacks are predicted to reach 324 million transactions in 2028, up from 261 million in 2025.

Ms Kutzner said this, paired with the ease of lodging a chargeback dispute, left businesses vulnerable.

"As a customer, I might as well click that button, that friendly button, and get my money back," she said.

Banks admit change is needed

The chief executive of the Australian Banking Association (ABA), Simon Birmingham acknowledges under current rules, small businesses are often let down.

" The ABA supports a comprehensive review of the scheme rules and fee settings so the system fairly balances the interests of both buyers and sellers. "

Simon Birmingham supports a review of chargeback legislation. (Supplied: ABA)

That would need to be done by the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA), which acknowledges chargebacks have become a concern for a number of businesses.

The RBA regulates the Payment Systems (Regulation) Act 1998, and as it stands, does not include much detail about chargeback processes.

The RBA had an opportunity to change this during its recent Retail Payments Regulation review, where changes to credit and debit surcharging were announced.

But little attention was given to the topic of chargebacks.

Payment experts like Ms Kutzner are waiting to see if the topic will be prioritised over the coming months after the RBA announced its next Payments System Regulation review last month.

A chargeback from AI

As artificial intelligence continues to accelerate, Ms Kutzner said it was only a matter of time before it formed part of our online research and shopping processes.

Return to sender Australian online sales are surging, but so are returns, and many retailers are wearing the cost of customers buying before trying.

Earlier this year, the trial of a new payment product was launched, known as agentic commerce.

It involves AI agents researching, comparing, booking and buying products on your behalf online.

While that may allow for efficiency for a household or business, Ms Kutzner warns it's unclear what will happen when a chargeback dispute is lodged.

AI hallucinations When a journalist emails a company with questions looking for answers, the least they expect is a real person to feed them the spin, half-truths or outright lies. Not a machine.

"It comes with multiple issues, for example, what if it got you the wrong category tickets or purchased on the wrong date," she said.

" The current process doesn't allow for a third party to be wrong. "

If the chargeback dispute process is already proving difficult between two people, what happens when new tech is the one actually at fault?

Who takes responsibility then?

Loading

And as AI becomes more entwined with the everyday, Ms Kutzner warns reviewing chargeback dispute processes and protections needs to be a matter of urgency, before the shiny technology becomes the new normal.

World.title: This woman sued for pregnancy discrimination and won. Her case is rare
World.content:
Australia has made massive progress in gender equality; more women are employed today than ever before.

But from corporations to warehouses, pregnant women and new mothers are routinely let go from their jobs, discriminated against, and in one case, forced to pump breastmilk in a storeroom and carry it home in a suitcase.

Tatiana Duarte was denied unpaid parental leave, flexible work, and support to breastfeed while working as a waiter and cleaner at the Consulate of the United Arab Emirates in Melbourne.

"My colleagues found me a storage room," she said.

"I didn't even have a table or a seat to breastfeed or anywhere to store my milk.

" I had to buy a suitcase with ice just to keep it cold so it wouldn't do any damage to my baby. "

Ms Duarte said the experience left her feeling "frustrated, sad and disappointed".

"Australia is supposed to be a country where you're meant to have rights," she said.

"I didn't expect this to happen."

Tatiana Duarte's legal action paid off, but her case is rare. (Supplied: Tatiana Duarte)

This year, Ms Duarte won a landmark discrimination case against her employer, and was awarded more than $200,000 in damages.

A case like this is rare — this kind of legal action is expensive, hard to navigate, and takes time.

Because Ms Duarte could not afford a lawyer, Victoria Legal Aid took on her case.

"There were so many delays, but finally we got it," she said.

Pregnancy discrimination cases reveal 'just the tip of the iceberg'

Despite pregnancy discrimination being unlawful for more than 30 years, the problem is still rife in Australia.

Dominique Allen, an anti-discrimination law researcher from Monash University, said pregnant women at all levels of employment were reporting unfair treatment.

"There are a few cases heard by courts, but we know that that is just the tip of the iceberg," she said.

"We found that it almost didn't matter if it was a small employer versus a large employer or across different industries, pregnancy discrimination was occurring regardless."

Professor Allen heard several stories from women facing this discrimination during her research, which found it occurred regardless of how long a person had been employed, their seniority, whether they were working full-time, or the sector they worked in.

In 2024, around 1,200 women responded to a survey by the University of South Australia's Centre for Workplace Excellence.

The results revealed a disturbing statistic — more than 91 per cent of them were discriminated against when they returned to work, and 89 per cent when pregnant at work.

"I was a manager in a government organisation and was told if I wanted flexible work hours perhaps, I should work at a supermarket," one woman told the researchers.

"I was told I wouldn't want to return to work as I would be 'clucky'," another said.

" My career was severely impacted by my pregnancy, and I was forced to give up my team leader role. "

A common theme among women experiencing this discrimination is that at such a vulnerable time in their life, they cannot take on the extra burden of fighting an employer.

As a result, many cases go unheard, making this an invisible problem in Australia.

We want to hear from you

Have you been discriminated against at work because you were pregnant or a new parent?

Did you experience health consequences as a result?

Have you worked in an organisation that perpetuated this discrimination?

World.title: ‘Absolute chaos’: Thousands of people rush across Moroccan border, hoping to get to Europe
World.content:
Breaking WorldEuropeImmigration ‘Absolute chaos’: Thousands of people rush across Moroccan border, hoping to get to Europe David Crowe July 31, 2026 — 5:24am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Thousands of migrants have rushed across the border from Morocco into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta in a startling move that was relayed on social media and triggered a political row about migration into Europe. One security official declared the border checkpoint had “totally collapsed” under pressure from the crowd, as young men spread instructions on social media on how to enter the Spanish territory on the northern coast of Africa. Some migrants swam from Moroccan territory to reach the Spanish enclave, while others walked around a breakwater and crossed the rocks in numbers that overwhelmed authorities. The political impact reached far beyond Spain because of the debate across Europe about migration, with British right-wing leader Nigel Farage sharing the dramatic videos online.



“It’s time to wake up everybody,” Farage declared. Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez promised an “immediate response” to the situation, as his critics blamed his migration laws for encouraging people to seek asylum in Spain and gain work rights in the European Union. Thousands of people flood the border. AP Photo/Antonio Sempere “We are mobilising all necessary resources, working with Moroccan and international authorities, and preparing the necessary measures to restore normalcy as soon as possible,” Sanchez said. Spain’s government later said it would send the military to help the Civil Guard “to maintain security in the city of Ceuta”.



Spanish newspaper El Pais reported that Civil Guard officers had to open the gates because they needed to prevent a bottleneck forming at the checkpoint. The rush follows a Supreme Court decision in Spain last month that protects migrants who are intercepted at sea while seeking to get to Ceuta, preventing them from being immediately returned to Morocco. Migrants cross from Morocco into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta. AP Photo/Antonio Sempere That ruling is being blamed by some politicians for giving Moroccans an incentive to swim to Ceuta, a distance of about 2 kilometres across the water, or walk around the breakwater. Another source of debate is the Sanchez government’s decision this year to grant an amnesty to migrants who were already in the country, leading to more than 1.3 million people applying to stay permanently.



Ceuta, located roughly opposite Gibraltar in the western Mediterranean, has been a Spanish territory since 1580 and now has the status of an autonomous city of Spain, although it is surrounded by Moroccan territory. Rachid Sbihi, the head of the association that represents the Spanish Civil Guard officers in Ceuta, called for a national emergency to be declared in Madrid to stop the mass movement because the border had totally collapsed. Spanish police officers respond as migrants cross from Morocco. AP Photo/Antonio Sempere “The situation is absolute chaos,” he said. “It’s not possible to give precise numbers, but there are thousands of migrants crossing.” The Ministry of the Interior in Madrid has pushed back at the idea of a national emergency being declared.



Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska is due to travel to Ceuta on Friday. The Mayor-President of Ceuta, Juan Jesús Vivas, said the influx had overwhelmed the city’s ⁠reception system and left hundreds of migrants sleeping outside. “We are facing a situation ​of absolute humanitarian and social emergency,” Vivas told radio station Cadena SER, adding that facilities for ​unaccompanied minors were operating at 2400 per cent of capacity. In comments to radio station Onda Cero, he described the situation as a national emergency and called for a “decisive, forceful, immediate and coordinated” response under a ​single command structure.



Arrivals were currently averaging about 300 people a day, according to Vivas. At that pace, he warned, Ceuta could face a situation comparable to the May 2021 migration crisis, when 10,000 people entered ​the enclave in mere ​days. Vivas also pointed ⁠to the human cost of the crossings, saying 60 bodies had been recovered at sea in recent months, and argued that ​stronger migration controls would help prevent further deaths. World.title: ASX set to jump, Microsoft leads Wall Street rally; Apple results ahead
World.content:
BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to jump, Microsoft leads Wall Street rally; Apple results ahead Stan Choe July 31, 2026 — 5:16am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

US stocks are rebounding after Microsoft leaped on hopes that its big spending on AI is translating into profits, while computer-chip companies clawed back some of their sharp recent losses. The S&P 500 rallied 1.5 per cent and recovered nearly all of its drop from the prior day, which was its worst in seven weeks. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was up 555 points, or 1.1 per cent in mid-afternoon trade. The Nasdaq composite, which is full of artificial-intelligence stocks, jumped 2.6 per cent a day after it fell 9.8 per cent below its record set last month. Technology stocks continue to drive the direction of Wall Street. Bloomberg The Australian sharemarket is set to jump, with futures pointing to a gain of 98 points, or 1.1 per cent, at the open. The ASX lost 0.8 per cent on Thursday. The Australian dollar was stronger at US70.35¢. Microsoft led the way and leaped 17 per cent after reporting a stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected. Growth was strong for its Azure cloud business, and CEO Satya Nadella said it reflects how customers are using Microsoft to move into AI.



Perhaps just as importantly for Wall Street, Microsoft did not announce a big increase in how much it plans to spend on AI investments, something that several other Big Tech rivals have done. Worries are high that such spending is eating into companies’ cash flows and may not ultimately be worth it if AI does not produce as much productivity and profits as promised. Meta Platforms helped demonstrate such fears after falling 9 per cent. The parent company of Facebook and Instagram reported a weaker profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected, even though it made slightly more in revenue than expected. It also raised the lower end of its forecasted range for spending on investments this year. Related Article Opinion

Interest rates As the Fed sits tight on interest rates, investors take action Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Companies involved in the making of the computer memory and processors that such “hyperscalers” are buying rose, recovering some of the big losses they’ve taken on worries that their stock prices shot too high in the euphoria around AI. Micron Technology jumped 17.6 per cent, for example, to trim its loss for the week to 5.6 per cent. It was one of the strongest forces lifting the S&P 500 after Microsoft.



Lam Research, a supplier to the semiconductor industry, soared 17.6 per cent after reporting stronger profit and revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected. Chip giant Advanced Micro Devices rallied 13.5 per cent. Apple results will be released after the closing bell. Jersey Mike’s Subs fell 4.4 per cent shortly after the sandwich chain made its market debut. Its IPO was priced at $US23. In the bond market, longer-term Treasury yields held a bit steadier following their sharp accelerations Wednesday. They had jumped after the chairman of the Federal Reserve, Kevin Warsh, gave few clues about what the central bank will do with interest rates to combat the painfully high inflation that continues to hurt the country. Higher rates could keep a lid on inflation, but they can also slow the economy and undercut prices for stocks and other investments.



The yield on the 10-year Treasury held steady at 4.67 per cent from late Wednesday. The 30-year Treasury yield edged up to 5.21 per cent from 5.20 per cent, a day after it shot up from 5.09 per cent. They move with investors’ expectations for inflation and economic growth in upcoming years. Warsh reaffirmed on Wednesday the Fed wants to get inflation back down to 2 per cent, even though the central bank decided not to raise interest rates despite its remaining higher than that. He also implied the bond market may already be doing some of the Fed’s work to restrain inflation, and he pointed to how yields have climbed since the central bank’s last meeting six weeks earlier. That leaves investors questioning whether the Fed is prepared to act if inflation worsens, or whether it is relying on financial markets to achieve the same outcome, according to Seema Shah, chief global strategist at Principal Asset Management. “If investors conclude that the latter is true, the credibility of the Fed’s inflation-fighting commitment could come under increasing scrutiny. Arguably, it already is.” President Donald Trump, who nominated Warsh to lead the Fed, has argued for lower interest rates even though they could cause inflation to accelerate.



Reports released Thursday suggested the US economy’s growth slowed by more during the spring than economists expected. A measure of Inflation, meanwhile, remained worse last month than the Federal Reserve’s target, but it slowed from May. In the oil market, prices eased back. Related Article Opinion

Home loans Buckle up for the banks’ mortgage war! Home loans have fallen off a cliff Elizabeth Knight Business columnist Brent crude, the international standard, fell 1.2 per cent to $US87.01 per barrel. It had swung as low as $US72 early this month and as high as $US102 last week on uncertainty about whether the United States and Iran could reach a deal to allow oil tankers to move freely again from the Middle East to customers worldwide. In stock markets worldwide, indexes rose in Europe following a mixed finish in Asia. South Korea’s Kospi fell 1.2 per cent, and France’s CAC 40 rose 0.9 per cent for two of the world’s bigger moves.



Seoul’s market has been at the centre of the huge recent moves for AI stocks because it’s dominated by two tech titans, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix. After more than doubling through this year’s first six months, the Kospi has plunged 34 per cent so far in July. Its drop on Thursday came as Samsung Electronics dipped 0.7 per cent. The tech giant reported a record profit for the spring and said demand for its chips continues to outpace supply, but its earnings nevertheless fell shy of analysts’ high expectations. World.content:
BusinessCompaniesCommercial real estate Historic Clifton Hill pub on the market after failed development bid Nicole Lindsay July 31, 2026 — 5:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Capital Gain The Royal Hotel in Clifton Hill is on the market for the first time in four decades and nearly 10 years since the front bar was open. The move comes three years after its owners, the Gudic family, lost their bid to build a five-storey apartment project over the historic corner hotel. For sale: the Royal Hotel on the corner of Spensley and Berry streets, Clifton Hill. Built in 1889, the three-storey hotel at 35-41 Spensley Street is on a 736-square-metre corner site in the heart of the Clifton Hill village and includes 29 rented rooms on the top floors. A gin distillery currently occupies some of the space and operates the bottleshop, but the pub is ripe for a new publican prepared to revamp the historic site.



Neighbours were outraged in 2019 when the Gudics lodged a bid for a residential project above the once-loved but shuttered pub in the enclave east of Hoddle Street. Colliers agents Ben Baines and Lucas Soccio are running the September 10 auction campaign and expect a price in the mid-$5 million range. Related Article City life Spawned from inner-city muck, this suburb full of lawyers is getting younger “There’s nothing better than a corner hotel in a village setting,” Baines said. Records show the Gudic family bought the pub in 1985 from Carlton & United Breweries with “5000 class 52 redeemable preference shares”. If that sounds like a complex way to buy a pub, it’s worth remembering CUB was taken over by Elders IXL in 1983 during the heady “corporate raider” period of management heralded by the late John Elliot.



Stingo Down Hoddle Street into Collingwood, investor Joe Awad has snapped up the Yorkshire Stingo Hotel for $2.5 million, a deal which reflects a skinny 3.82 per cent yield. The City East Motel behind it fetched $3.5 million. It’s not quite the total $8 million result that was hoped for the two properties. The pub, at 40-48 Hoddle Street, and the motel, at 181 Langridge Street, were bought by the Freeman family in 1988 for $130,000. The Yorkshire Stingo, on the corner of Hoddle and Langridge streets. Both properties cover 1136 square metres of land and were earmarked for a development along with another 1121 square metres at the rear. Those three warehouses, at 197-203 Landgridge Street, were owned by Munro Shoes – one of the last remaining shoe manufacturers in Abbotsford – and sold for $3 million. Stonebridge’s Max Warren, Dylan Kilner, Nic Hage and Chao Zhang handled negotiations.



Chinatown Last month’s hot auction in Chinatown, where 172-176 Little Bourke Street sold for $6.11 million, has inspired a clutch of owners to test the market with their own long-held properties. First up is 179 Russell Street, which is going to auction on August 26. The 180-square-metre two-level building is on a 102-square-metre piece of the city and is expected to fetch more than $3 million. It’s got a new lease and fitout to Jin Noodle Restaurant, which pays $165,000 a year in rent. 179 Russell Street, in Melbourne’s Chinatown district. Records show it last sold in 1994 for $1.05 million. Savills agents Julian Heatherich and Tom O’Halloran, with the Di Petta Group’s Winnie Chow, are running the auction campaign.



On August 27, the loveliest of the lot, 107 Little Bourke Street goes under the hammer. Designed by one of Melbourne’s best architects, Nahum Barnett, in 1903, the three-storey building last changed hands in 1970 for $27,000. It’s on a 99-square-metre parcel of land and rented to Khao Soi Melbourne. Lemon Baxter’s Hans Fan expects it to sell for about $4.8 million, which equates to a yield of 4.1 per cent. 107 Little Bourke Street, in Melbourne’s Chinatown district. Next month, 218-220 Little Bourke Street will be up for auction after 70 years in the one family’s hands. The double-storey shop of 325 square metres is expected to sell for about $4 million on September 3.



The building has a 10-year lease, with a 10-year option to the Lost Bar, which pays just under $180,000 a year in rent. Records show a quarter-share in the building last changed hands in 2004 for $500,000 and in 1970, a half-stake was transferred for $32,000. Fitzroys’ Lewis Waddell, Ben Liu and David Bourke are running the auction. According to Fitzroys’ latest Walk the CBD report, Chinatown vacancies nearly halved in the past year to 3.5 per cent from 6.6 per cent. 218-220 Little Bourke Street, Melbourne. There are a clutch of cafes and restaurants for sale along the west end too but not at auction.



Brendan Sullivan is selling the freehold of the long-running Grain Store restaurant at 517 Flinders Lane. Sullivan has been progressively selling the office and retail complex on Flinders Lane, which he bought in 2011 from the Smorgon family for $16.35 million. CBRE’s Alex Brierley, Nathan Mufale and Jing Jun Heng have the listing and expect about $3 million. At 540 Little Collins Street, the freehold of the Five Points bagel outlet is also for sale and expected to sell for about $1 million through Fitzroys’ Waddell and Liu. The Grain Store at 517 Flinders Lane. Lemon Baxter’s Fans and Paul O’Sullivan are also selling the Jumbo Kebabs freehold at 200 Spencer Street, opposite Southern Cross Station. It has a $1.95 million price tag.



Sculptor The North Melbourne laneway studio of the renowned late sculptor Erwin Fabian is up for sale. Fabian, born in Berlin in 1915, travelled to Australia in the 1940s on the ship the Dunera after escaping Nazi Germany in 1938. He joined the Australian Army’s education unit during World War II before returning to London for 12 years. He came back to Australia as a sculptor working with found pieces of metal. Inside the North Melbourne studio of sculptor Erwin Fabian. Fabian, whose work was described as “conceptual illusionism” by art professor Sasha Grishin, died in 2020.



The studio of 117 square metres is off Arden Street at 3-5 Wylies Lane, in the central pocket between Curzon and Errol streets. It’s on 152 square metres of land and goes to auction on August 27. Simpsons agents Richard Simpson and Ariana McCarron expect between $900,000 and $990,000 for the property. “Artwork not included” is the disappointing postscript to the Simpsons ad. Armadale redux Armadale’s blue-chip High Street has another large property up for sale, a 1990s office building halfway between Glenferrie and Kooyong roads. Records show the vendors of 1113-1121 High Street paid $3.45 million in 1996 and are looking at a payday of about $13.5 million.



113-1121 High Street, Armadale The 1589-square-metre building has five shops at street level, four offices upstairs and 61 car spaces. It’s on a large site of 1363 square metres. It has three agents on the case: Cushman & Wakefield’s Oliver Hay, Maker Property’s George Davies and Gross Waddell ICR’s Alex Ham. Last week, 935-951 High Street, on 1373 square metres, hit the market with a price tag of about $15.5 million and a permit for an apartment project. World.title: We think our boss has become obsessed with a chatbot. What can we do?
World.content:
BusinessWorkplaceWork therapy Opinion We think our boss has become obsessed with a chatbot. What can we do? Jonathan Rivett Careers contributor July 31, 2026 — 5:01am

July 31, 2026 — 5:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

I used to have a strong professional relationship with my boss and I respected them. But they have changed recently. Once they were considerate and supportive – some colleagues even thought they were a bit too gentle. Now they are neither of those things. They are definitely not gentle. They have started talking about instituting a new regime based on the advice of a friend and business mentor. All the new policies and ideas seem severe. A small group of people who report to this boss (including me) have talked in private about who this “mentor” is and why they are telling our manager to be so harsh and punishing. Our team is performing well, and has for years. There is now a strong rumour that the friend is actually an AI chatbot. Surely, that can’t be true, can it? There could be any number of reasons for how this has come about. John Shakespeare It certainly seems extraordinary that a professional could become so attached to a chatbot that they would change their entire work style and personality based on its “opinion”. Extraordinary but not inconceivable. About three years ago, a reader wrote to me about a work problem that they had reported to their HR team. They had been rudely brushed off. When they experimentally asked a chatbot about the same problem, the AI response was infinitely more empathetic and sensitive.



Although we can put this down to the tendency of modern large language model (LLM) chatbots to validate and endorse the concerns or ideas of its user, partly as a way of keeping the conversation going, an unflattering term like “AI sycophancy” doesn’t change the experience of that reader. Or anyone who speaks with AI and finds “someone” who appears to genuinely listen. I’m not going to say I know for sure what is going on with your boss. They may not be consulting a chatbot at all (although I find the evidence proposed in your longer email, via your worried colleagues, compelling). But to answer your direct question: yes, it can absolutely be true. People today are anthropomorphising AI in all sorts of different ways – this is no longer a fringe practice. Some people develop what are known as parasocial relationships with this new generation of ultra-coherent AI models. “Parasocial interaction” is a term coined in the 1950s to describe, for example, the way a TV viewer might come to think of a media personality as their friend, despite the relationship being entirely one-way. Now, some experts in the field believe “parasocial” is not quite the right term to apply to profound relationships between humans and AI. Whereas in the ’50s a TV presenter might inadvertently (or at least perfunctorily) encourage parasocial intimacy by looking down the camera and talking directly to the audience, in the 2020s a chatbot mimics interest, understanding and even love in a highly sophisticated, often utterly earnest, way.



Let’s stick with the term for now, at any rate. Editor's pick Opinion

Work therapy My colleague is constantly negative. How can I make them cheer up? Jonathan Rivett Careers contributor We know that people today are anthropomorphising AI in all sorts of different ways – this is no longer a fringe practice. They converse with their favourite chatbot as they might a human therapist, a companion, a “troubleshooter” and even a “work buddy”. If your boss is doing that, but has entered into a pathological version of parasocial engagement, it’s quite possible that they’re taking advice from this digital confidant in good faith, genuinely understanding it to be their intimate. And perhaps their teller of cold, hard truths. There could be any number of reasons for how this has come about. It might have been a conversational chain reaction, beginning with a benign question but branching, exchange by exchange, into something much more radical.



Or it may have been less accidental. Perhaps your boss, worried that they were seen as a soft touch, sought advice on changing this perception, and were given a menu of aggressive and ruthless management tactics. The change won’t have come out of nowhere. And while I think it’s sensible to be curious about, and even sympathetic to, what catalysed it, you don’t need to tolerate or excuse the cold-hearted turn. Your manager, of course, has the prerogative to make changes, and is under no obligation to be your friend, but if they’re taking dogmatic advice from a chatbot, I think they’re engaging in an ill-advised, even dangerous practice – and possibly stepping onto legally shaky ground. One day in the future consulting with robots as if they’re trustworthy humans might be entirely normal, and possibly beneficial. That day has not arrived. Send your questions through to Work Therapy by emailing jonathan@theinkbureau.com.au Get workplace news, advice and perspectives to help make your job work for you.

World.title: Priscilla’s pub to get a $5 million facelift by its new operator
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesCommercial real estate Priscilla’s pub to get a $5 million facelift by its new operator Carolyn Cummins July 31, 2026 — 5:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Capital Gain The Imperial Erskineville, in Sydney’s inner west – one of the venues featured in the film The Adventures of Priscilla, Queen of the Desert – is getting a facelift to take the venue into its next phase. Odd Culture Group is the new operator and will work with the owners, Universal Hotels, to give the “Impy”, as it is affectionately known, a $5 million renovation that will see its ground floor double in size, through an expanded beer garden as well as a 24-hour basement bar. The Imperial Erskineville is getting a major makeover. James Brickwood Universal Hotels acquired the Impy in 2023 for about $20 million from The Sydney Collective’s Fraser Short and Australian Hotels Association NSW President Scott Leach who saved the site from closure in 2015.



Constructed in 1880, the Impy at 35 Erskineville Road, has been an institution and symbol of the queer community over many years of its operations. Last year, the venue was also added to the NSW State Heritage Register for its “deep cultural and historical significance”. Editor's pick Commercial real estate Will it be third try lucky for controversial car park in exclusive Double Bay? Odd Culture, known for its portfolio of inclusive and diverse venues across Sydney, is an operator of other Universal Hotels’ venues, including the Universal, The Oxford and The Riley pubs, and is run by founder and chief executive James Thorpe. He said the aim of the renovations is to secure both groups’ “long-term investment in the future of queer nightlife and artistic expression in Sydney”. “The Imperial has spent more than 40 years helping to shape Sydney’s queer culture. This redevelopment is one of the biggest investments in its history, but more importantly, it’s an investment in the next 40 years,” Thorpe said.



It’s business as usual at the Impy with Odd Culture taking the reins from September 1, with the renovations slated to start in early 2027. Arnaout’s Wisemans Inn Fresh from his $500 million sale of seven regional pubs, Iris Capital’s Sam Arnaout is selling his Wisemans Inn Hotel on the banks of the Hawkesbury River, north-west of Sydney. The Wisemans Inn Hotel. Arnaout bought the 195-year-old pub in September 2022 from Bill Young for about $10 million and is divesting it as part of his plan to focus on Sydney-based projects.



The pub opened in 1827 on a 5123-square-metre landholding and includes accommodation comprising six freestanding motel suites and five boutique pub rooms. The venue generates about $3.2 million in annual turnover. It is close to a new boat ramp with 163 bays, but there is potential for expanded al fresco dining, family-friendly spaces, and special events programming. JLL Hotels & Hospitality Group agents Kate MacDonald, Greg Jeloudev and Ben McDonald are advising on the sale. Seven Hills The former Mercedes-Benz processing and parts storage centre in Seven Hills is being sold by the private vendor SHMPC Pty Limited with price expectations of $25 million to $27 million. Constructed in 2018, the 29 Brumby Street site is being offered with vacant possession in the short term and comprises 5408 sq m of office and warehouse facilities on a 9703 sq m general industrial landholding and sits in the Blacktown City Council zone.



The property currently generates net rental income of about $1.46 million per annum. It is purpose-built for vehicle-intensive operations and comes with a 100kW solar system. Colliers’ Paul McGlynn is advising on the sale. 29 Brumby Street, Seven Hills. NRL hotel With the tom-toms beating in the jungle that the National Rugby League is scouting Sydney for a new hotel, the hospitality sector is proving a happy hunting ground for investors and owners. While no details have emerged, the Australian Rugby League Commission chairman Peter V’landys said recently that the NRL was looking to boost its property empire to be worth about $1 billion.



It has been suggested the NRL is looking at the Novotel Sydney International Airport hotel based in Wolli Creek. If the deal is done, it will add to its existing portfolio in Sydney which includes the Quest Woolooware Bay. It also owns the ibis Styles Port Macquarie hotel. The potential sale comes as hotels continue to scoop up property awards. Last month, the Surry Hills Village by TOGA which includes the Eve Hotel won the Urban Taskforce Australia’s 2026 Development of the Year. At the Accommodation Australia NSW Awards for Excellence held last week, the Luxury Hotel of the Year award was won by Park Hyatt Sydney, while the Metropolitan Deluxe Hotel of the Year went to Sheraton Grand Sydney Hyde Park. carolynannecummins@gmail.com The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. World.title: The Melbourne intersection that epitomises where our road safety approach is going wrong
World.content:
We live in Melbourne’s inner west. I drive a hatchback, but commute by bike. Our son has been learning to drive for the last year. Recently, turning right at a quiet intersection, he panicked. There was no hazard; just traffic lights without a right-turn arrow. In a year of supervised driving, our ultra-controlled road system had so thoroughly insulated him that he’d never been required to exercise his own judgment in this everyday scenario.

As a professional designer, this was a red flag. In my industry, we practise user-centred design in which we distil and design for the user’s core purpose, and minimise any factors that impede this. The core purpose of any road system is to move from A to B as safely, economically and efficiently as possible. But Victoria’s “Safe System” framework has abandoned this balance. Physical and prescriptive impediments to our road system’s core function are being rolled out without restraint. More frustratingly, we’re being asked to endure a lot of usability pain for almost no safety gain.

Peak compliance: The Macaulay Road level crossing in Kensington has more than 10 different signs competing for attention. Steve Martinuzzo

In design, it’s a failure if the core function of a system is compromised by other objectives. If I designed a medical device that was totally safe but didn’t work, I’d be out of a job. Yet, by trying to micro-control everything, this is exactly what our road authorities are doing. And by treating the human driver as a liability rather than an accountable citizen, our roads and policies are becoming increasingly incongruent to the community they should support.

Good information design relies on visual hierarchy, which means telling the user just what they need to know at the moment they need to know it. No less, and definitely no more. However, today’s roads break every rule of visual information design.

World.title: Mystery death of the original ‘gymfluencer’: Inside the tragic final days of Zyzz
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

You can’t miss Aziz “Zyzz” Shavershian’s headstone in a grassy corner of Riverstone cemetery in Sydney’s north-west. There he is, looking back at you from an oval ceramic photo set in the granite, a muscular bicep straining against the fabric of his tight black T-shirt, all tousled, gelled hair and coal-black eyes, against an image of a tranquil ocean meeting an endless blue summer sky. Etched beneath the dates of his short life – March 24, 1989 to August 5, 2011 – is Zyzz’s signature mantra, Veni, Vidi, Vici (“I came, I saw, I conquered”) that in life was tattooed across his hairless, sculpted chest. Over the years, a steady stream of local and overseas fans have made the pilgrimage here, to lay flowers and cards on the polished granite base under the gum trees, or post videos on commemorative pages on Instagram, YouTube and Facebook (one such page has 346,000 followers). Many of the tributes left on these digital shrines are overwhelmingly effusive. “Thank you for changing mine and a million other lives,” a visitor from Seattle posted on Instagram. “After 12 years, I finally made it to your grave. It was an honour to pay my respects,” declared a muscly, tattooed compatriot on Instagram. “You motivated me to get off the couch and get to the gym,” gushed one Australian man on YouTube. Back in 2010 and 2011, before TikTok and Snapchat, before Instagram became popular, and before the reign of the insidious algorithms that would turn social media into an endless echo-chamber, Zyzz racked up hundreds of thousands of views for his videos on YouTube and a loyal follower base on bodybuilding forums and his Facebook page. Aziz “Zyzz’ Shavershian at his gym in Sydney’s Carlingford at age 19. @zyzz_page_official/Instagram A skinny, shy World of Warcraft gamester and star high-school student who metamorphosed into a muscly party boy, Aziz brought the classic nerd-to-superman archetype to life through Zyzz, baiting his legion of young male followers to “get aesthetic” in videos shot from his bedroom webcam or by members of his crew while he was partying or sweating it out in the gym. The videos were always amateurish, often fun, sometimes cringeworthy, occasionally offensive, but they resonated. After his death, Zyzz became more popular and mythologised than he ever was in life. By the standards of today’s vast army of bulked-up online gym influencers (“gymfluencers”) – the top tier of whom can earn in the millions – Zyzz was as lean as a lamp post, but that was precisely his bedrock appeal. Because his transformation from teen beanpole to sculpted Adonis didn’t shout steroid-bolstered size (even though he did use image-enhancing drugs), his muscle growth at least seemed plausible – albeit one attributable to a mighty amount of grit, hard work and self-discipline. Which is why his signature mantra, “We’re all gonna make it, brahs,” became a rallying cry. Some credit Zyzz and his “aesthetics crew”, which included his older brother, Said Shavershian, who adopted the name of Chestbrah, with upending the world of bodybuilding, shifting the focus away from sheer size and thickness to a tight, V-shaped physique. “At that time, bodybuilding was still a cult sport that only attracted guys with superior genetics and a desire to put on bulk,” recalls Said, who is now 40 and runs a successful online training business supported by more than 437,000 followers on Instagram. “We changed the game by showing people that you don’t need to be an overblown bodybuilder to look good. Most men dream of having a physique like Brad Pitt in Troy or Zac Efron in Baywatch, but not every man wants to look like Arnold Schwarzenegger.”



As Zyzz’s online star rose, so did the online backlash from trolls calling him a wanker, a gym douche, and a “fake natty” (someone who is using steroids but pretends to be natural). And not surprisingly, given he invited fans and haters alike to admire his physique (“You mirin’ brah?“), he also became a magnet for competitive hostility from other men – and, sometimes, outright aggression. On one occasion, according to his brother, he was set upon by a bunch of hoons outside a nightclub; he briefly fended them off and jumped into a passing taxi, but before the vehicle sped away, his attackers shoved their arms through the window and tried to wrench him out. While he publicly dismissed the vitriol with bravado – “I’d rather be a person that’s hated on, than a person that does the hating” – there were signs that the deeply vulnerable young man was increasingly undone by it. For a man obsessed with his appearance, the cruel attacks on his facial features, most notably his prominent nose, must have particularly stung. Related Article Good Weekend Elijah was 10 when his friend typed ‘porn’ into a search engine. He was afraid – but unable to look away The relentless demand for more and better content, combined with a lifestyle of nightclubs, music festivals and heavy training – all fuelled by a volatile cocktail of steroids, recreational drugs and Xanax – began to take its toll, leaving Aziz utterly exhausted by his own alter-ego creation within just 18 months or so. “There is no ‘Zyzz’, that is just an act,” he posted in a revealing video in the months before his death. When news broke in August 2011 that the 22-year-old internet phenomenon had died in Thailand – reportedly in a sauna, from a previously undiagnosed heart condition – public speculation ran wild. Was the cardiac arrest caused by steroid use, recreational drugs in the sauna or an underlying, unmanaged heart condition? Some days later, when it was revealed that a thief had stolen belongings from Aziz’s hotel room – including his laptop, wallet and clothes – conspiracy theories flourished. Behind the tragic headlines, the truth never entirely came out. Now, as the 15th anniversary of Aziz’s death approaches, a new documentary to be aired from August 5 on Stan (owned by Nine Entertainment, the owners of this masthead) explores the rise of the self-proclaimed “son of Zeus and brother of Hercules”. Poster Boy: Becoming Zyzz contains some dramatic new information about his death (we’ll get to this a bit later), including his real reason for going to Thailand, and some morbidly compelling medical details about what killed him.



Aziz and Said Shavershian probably would not have made it to Australia had it not been for the collapse of the Soviet Union in the early 1990s and the elder brother’s severe childhood asthma. Having lost most of their assets in the upheaval and seeking a warmer, drier climate for Said’s condition, the boys’ Russian-Kurdish parents, both of whom were doctors in Moscow, moved to Australia in 1993, when Said was seven and Aziz four, finally settling in Sydney’s Carlingford, a family-friendly, middle-class area in the city’s north-west. Theirs was the classic migrant tale of starting afresh and building a new life which, for the parents, meant getting their degrees again. They had high hopes for their sons, wanting them to be doctors or lawyers, but fortune took them in another direction. Both brothers had lingering lisps when they were small; unable to pronounce Aziz, older brother Said called him “Zyzz” and the nickname stuck. At Marist College in Eastwood, an all-boys Catholic school, the brothers were as academically impressive as they were athletically unassuming, with Aziz distinguishing himself as the school’s dux. The boys grew up watching WWE – their heroes were Hulk Hogan and Ultimate Warrior – and geeked out over games like Warcraft. As the high school years advanced, the professional hopes of the parents took a back seat as the boys found a physical outlet in the gym. “I started bodybuilding because I was bullied a bit in school for being so skinny,” Said tells Good Weekend. “So I wanted to build a bit of muscle mass to look intimidating to other men, and also get the attention of girls.” Aziz soon followed his brother to the gym and found his natural home there. “He started getting bigger than me, and I didn’t know why,” Said told Neil “The Muscle” Cummins, a former Kings Cross bouncer, in a frank interview last year for Cummins’ Secrets of the Underworld podcast. “And then I walked in on him putting a needle in his bum. And I’m like, ‘You little f-----, you’ve been doing this behind my back.’ “Around year 11, he started learning about girls and drugs, and it went downhill from there,” Said also told Cummins. “He was very hard to control. Even my parents couldn’t control him.” Phillip Raymond, who became a friend of Aziz during this time, trained with him at Fitness First in Carlingford, and also filmed content for his videos. He says Aziz had charisma in spades. “Girls wanted to be with him and guys wanted to hang out with him,” he recalls. What didn’t come across in his boisterous videos was Aziz’s intelligence. “He was super-intelligent, very switched on.” Loading



Given that Aziz, at 185 centimetres tall and super skinny, had the type of frame that in gym parlance is a “hard-gainer”, his transformation, via high-volume, heavy resistance training, would have taken years without chemical enhancement. Phillip Raymond explains that he never had to resort to steroids because, with a shorter (he’s 170 centimetres), thicker, mesomorphic physique, he has always been able to pack on muscle quickly. But Aziz was a young man in a hurry – he wanted the dream physique and appeared to relish the image of the hypermasculine alpha male that can accompany it, even if it was just that: an image. “You lift weights, you get tatts, you f--- bitches, brah,” he once crudely boasted to his fans in a video. Selina Miles, director of Poster Boy, whose award-winning documentary Silenced focused on the fight against laws silencing sexual-abuse survivors, told Good Weekend she was determined not to skate over Zyzz’s at times boorish braggadocio. “I couldn’t promise participants we wouldn’t be looking at that,” she says. “By the same token, it’s really important for audiences to remember he was 20 when he became famous and only 22 when he died. When you meet his friends, you think, ‘This guy must have been all right.’ Many of the people who loved him have grown into really self-aware, considerate men.” For years after Aziz’s death, Said was forced to be a reluctant apologist for his brother’s often distasteful stunts and statements, such as when Zyzz wore his T-shirt as a turban and mockingly mimicked prayer. Aziz was just being a “clown”, a “dickhead” under his Zyzz persona, Said told Neil Cummins. Said insisted that those alter-ego antics did not reflect his brother’s real-life views, that he had a diverse group of mates, including Muslims and gay friends. And despite his reputation as a playboy, which was “partly true”, Aziz had a steady girlfriend for three years. Over the past 15 years, Said has put considerable energy into preserving his younger brother’s name and complex legacy, most notably by producing a 19-minute YouTube video (Zyzz: The Legacy) that has attracted more than 18 million views. So in 2022, when documentary producer Tom Blackwell approached Said about making a documentary looking at Zyzz’s life, he pounced at the opportunity. “There’s a bit of Zyzz in all of us,” Aziz once declared. Said Shavershian, who is now 40, is intent on preserving his younger brother’s legacy. James Brickwood If anything, Aziz’s short life and his Zyzz persona serves as a mirror for a look-at-me selfie culture that has only grown exponentially more pervasive since his passing, reaching a new inflection point with the current phenomenon of “looksmaxxing”. (Said has been upfront on Instagram about his own enhancements: “Hair transplant: $10,000; Veneers $15,000; “Brotox” $500 for six months; Supps and TRT [testosterone replacement therapy], $500 per month.“) But the “looksmaxxing” terrain becomes very dubious – and dangerous – in extreme examples led by influencers such as Clavicular, who advocate bone injury and smashing to create a more chiselled jawline and cheekbones (there is no medical evidence backing these methods).



Daniel Principe, a high-profile youth advocate best known for his campaigns to promote healthy masculinity, was a little younger than Aziz when the Zyzz persona was riding high. “We all love a transformation story and Zyzz had an appeal, especially for guys who weren’t particularly sporty, jockish, or ladsy – he told us, ‘You, too, could achieve the ultimate physique,’” Principe recalls. “At the time, no one else was putting themselves out there like him. Now it’s a saturated market, with both the number of gym bros and fitness influencers.” It certainly looks that way: back in 2010, when Zyzz was pumping out sets on the bench-press at Fitness First in Carlingford, there were 800 gyms and fitness centres in Australia; today, there are more than 7300. For young men in particular, anything that drags them away from their screens has to be a good thing. Yet, Principe is disturbed by the sheer volume of “fitfluencers”, biohackers and celebrities who are injecting steroids and peptides to maintain a perfect body, while insisting to their followers they have achieved their results by hard training, diet and over-the-counter supplements. ‘Perhaps even the supplement sponsors don’t really care if an influencer is hiding their steroid use.’ Youth advocate Daniel Principe “Even if a young man suspects an influencer is on steroids, he can’t escape the visual saturation of images of ‘giga chads’ – idealised versions of alpha males – confronting him daily on platforms like TikTok and Instagram,” says Principe. “Perhaps even the supplement sponsors don’t really care if an influencer is hiding their steroid use because it’s like, ‘You’re helping me sell my product, so who cares?’ ” Related Article Good Weekend ‘What’s bubbling underneath’: Showing teen boys how to master emotion and empathy No generation in human history has spent more time watching, listening and interacting with their peers – and less time listening to their parents and older mentors – than people under 25 today, thanks to social media invading every corner of our lives, Principe points out. This makes the battle for parents, and mentors with wiser heads, more challenging than ever, he says. The underlying driver of all this self-obsession is something far more insidious than narcissism in the classical sense, according to research over the past few years: it’s constant body surveillance, fuelled by looking at social media feeds for hours every day. Far from motivating us to improve our lives – get out and exercise, eat healthily – we’re often left feeling anxious, inadequate and confused by the flood of images.

World.title: ‘Absolute chaos’: Thousands of people rush across Moroccan border, hoping to get to Europe
World.content:
Breaking WorldEuropeImmigration ‘Absolute chaos’: Thousands of people rush across Moroccan border, hoping to get to Europe David Crowe July 31, 2026 — 5:24am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Thousands of migrants have rushed across the border from Morocco into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta in a startling move that was relayed on social media and triggered a political row about migration into Europe. One security official declared the border checkpoint had “totally collapsed” under pressure from the crowd, as young men spread instructions on social media on how to enter the Spanish territory on the northern coast of Africa. Some migrants swam from Moroccan territory to reach the Spanish enclave, while others walked around a breakwater and crossed the rocks in numbers that overwhelmed authorities. The political impact reached far beyond Spain because of the debate across Europe about migration, with British right-wing leader Nigel Farage sharing the dramatic videos online.



“It’s time to wake up everybody,” Farage declared. Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez promised an “immediate response” to the situation, as his critics blamed his migration laws for encouraging people to seek asylum in Spain and gain work rights in the European Union. Thousands of people flood the border. AP Photo/Antonio Sempere “We are mobilising all necessary resources, working with Moroccan and international authorities, and preparing the necessary measures to restore normalcy as soon as possible,” Sanchez said. Spain’s government later said it would send the military to help the Civil Guard “to maintain security in the city of Ceuta”.



Spanish newspaper El Pais reported that Civil Guard officers had to open the gates because they needed to prevent a bottleneck forming at the checkpoint. The rush follows a Supreme Court decision in Spain last month that protects migrants who are intercepted at sea while seeking to get to Ceuta, preventing them from being immediately returned to Morocco. Migrants cross from Morocco into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta. AP Photo/Antonio Sempere That ruling is being blamed by some politicians for giving Moroccans an incentive to swim to Ceuta, a distance of about 2 kilometres across the water, or walk around the breakwater. Another source of debate is the Sanchez government’s decision this year to grant an amnesty to migrants who were already in the country, leading to more than 1.3 million people applying to stay permanently.



Ceuta, located roughly opposite Gibraltar in the western Mediterranean, has been a Spanish territory since 1580 and now has the status of an autonomous city of Spain, although it is surrounded by Moroccan territory. Rachid Sbihi, the head of the association that represents the Spanish Civil Guard officers in Ceuta, called for a national emergency to be declared in Madrid to stop the mass movement because the border had totally collapsed. Spanish police officers respond as migrants cross from Morocco. AP Photo/Antonio Sempere “The situation is absolute chaos,” he said. “It’s not possible to give precise numbers, but there are thousands of migrants crossing.” The Ministry of the Interior in Madrid has pushed back at the idea of a national emergency being declared.



Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska is due to travel to Ceuta on Friday. The Mayor-President of Ceuta, Juan Jesús Vivas, said the influx had overwhelmed the city’s ⁠reception system and left hundreds of migrants sleeping outside. “We are facing a situation ​of absolute humanitarian and social emergency,” Vivas told radio station Cadena SER, adding that facilities for ​unaccompanied minors were operating at 2400 per cent of capacity. In comments to radio station Onda Cero, he described the situation as a national emergency and called for a “decisive, forceful, immediate and coordinated” response under a ​single command structure.



Arrivals were currently averaging about 300 people a day, according to Vivas. At that pace, he warned, Ceuta could face a situation comparable to the May 2021 migration crisis, when 10,000 people entered ​the enclave in mere ​days. Vivas also pointed ⁠to the human cost of the crossings, saying 60 bodies had been recovered at sea in recent months, and argued that ​stronger migration controls would help prevent further deaths. World.title: ASX set to jump, Microsoft leads Wall Street rally; Apple results ahead
World.content:
BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to jump, Microsoft leads Wall Street rally; Apple results ahead Stan Choe July 31, 2026 — 5:16am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

US stocks are rebounding after Microsoft leaped on hopes that its big spending on AI is translating into profits, while computer-chip companies clawed back some of their sharp recent losses. The S&P 500 rallied 1.5 per cent and recovered nearly all of its drop from the prior day, which was its worst in seven weeks. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was up 555 points, or 1.1 per cent in mid-afternoon trade. The Nasdaq composite, which is full of artificial-intelligence stocks, jumped 2.6 per cent a day after it fell 9.8 per cent below its record set last month. Technology stocks continue to drive the direction of Wall Street. Bloomberg The Australian sharemarket is set to jump, with futures pointing to a gain of 98 points, or 1.1 per cent, at the open. The ASX lost 0.8 per cent on Thursday. The Australian dollar was stronger at US70.35¢. Microsoft led the way and leaped 17 per cent after reporting a stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected. Growth was strong for its Azure cloud business, and CEO Satya Nadella said it reflects how customers are using Microsoft to move into AI.



Perhaps just as importantly for Wall Street, Microsoft did not announce a big increase in how much it plans to spend on AI investments, something that several other Big Tech rivals have done. Worries are high that such spending is eating into companies’ cash flows and may not ultimately be worth it if AI does not produce as much productivity and profits as promised. Meta Platforms helped demonstrate such fears after falling 9 per cent. The parent company of Facebook and Instagram reported a weaker profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected, even though it made slightly more in revenue than expected. It also raised the lower end of its forecasted range for spending on investments this year. Related Article Opinion

Interest rates As the Fed sits tight on interest rates, investors take action Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Companies involved in the making of the computer memory and processors that such “hyperscalers” are buying rose, recovering some of the big losses they’ve taken on worries that their stock prices shot too high in the euphoria around AI. Micron Technology jumped 17.6 per cent, for example, to trim its loss for the week to 5.6 per cent. It was one of the strongest forces lifting the S&P 500 after Microsoft.



Lam Research, a supplier to the semiconductor industry, soared 17.6 per cent after reporting stronger profit and revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected. Chip giant Advanced Micro Devices rallied 13.5 per cent. Apple results will be released after the closing bell. Jersey Mike’s Subs fell 4.4 per cent shortly after the sandwich chain made its market debut. Its IPO was priced at $US23. In the bond market, longer-term Treasury yields held a bit steadier following their sharp accelerations Wednesday. They had jumped after the chairman of the Federal Reserve, Kevin Warsh, gave few clues about what the central bank will do with interest rates to combat the painfully high inflation that continues to hurt the country. Higher rates could keep a lid on inflation, but they can also slow the economy and undercut prices for stocks and other investments.



The yield on the 10-year Treasury held steady at 4.67 per cent from late Wednesday. The 30-year Treasury yield edged up to 5.21 per cent from 5.20 per cent, a day after it shot up from 5.09 per cent. They move with investors’ expectations for inflation and economic growth in upcoming years. Warsh reaffirmed on Wednesday the Fed wants to get inflation back down to 2 per cent, even though the central bank decided not to raise interest rates despite its remaining higher than that. He also implied the bond market may already be doing some of the Fed’s work to restrain inflation, and he pointed to how yields have climbed since the central bank’s last meeting six weeks earlier. That leaves investors questioning whether the Fed is prepared to act if inflation worsens, or whether it is relying on financial markets to achieve the same outcome, according to Seema Shah, chief global strategist at Principal Asset Management. “If investors conclude that the latter is true, the credibility of the Fed’s inflation-fighting commitment could come under increasing scrutiny. Arguably, it already is.” President Donald Trump, who nominated Warsh to lead the Fed, has argued for lower interest rates even though they could cause inflation to accelerate.



Reports released Thursday suggested the US economy’s growth slowed by more during the spring than economists expected. A measure of Inflation, meanwhile, remained worse last month than the Federal Reserve’s target, but it slowed from May. In the oil market, prices eased back. Related Article Opinion

Home loans Buckle up for the banks’ mortgage war! Home loans have fallen off a cliff Elizabeth Knight Business columnist Brent crude, the international standard, fell 1.2 per cent to $US87.01 per barrel. It had swung as low as $US72 early this month and as high as $US102 last week on uncertainty about whether the United States and Iran could reach a deal to allow oil tankers to move freely again from the Middle East to customers worldwide. In stock markets worldwide, indexes rose in Europe following a mixed finish in Asia. South Korea’s Kospi fell 1.2 per cent, and France’s CAC 40 rose 0.9 per cent for two of the world’s bigger moves.



Seoul’s market has been at the centre of the huge recent moves for AI stocks because it’s dominated by two tech titans, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix. After more than doubling through this year’s first six months, the Kospi has plunged 34 per cent so far in July. Its drop on Thursday came as Samsung Electronics dipped 0.7 per cent. The tech giant reported a record profit for the spring and said demand for its chips continues to outpace supply, but its earnings nevertheless fell shy of analysts’ high expectations. World.title: Historic Clifton Hill pub on the market after failed development bid
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesCommercial real estate Historic Clifton Hill pub on the market after failed development bid Nicole Lindsay July 31, 2026 — 5:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Capital Gain The Royal Hotel in Clifton Hill is on the market for the first time in four decades and nearly 10 years since the front bar was open. The move comes three years after its owners, the Gudic family, lost their bid to build a five-storey apartment project over the historic corner hotel. For sale: the Royal Hotel on the corner of Spensley and Berry streets, Clifton Hill. Built in 1889, the three-storey hotel at 35-41 Spensley Street is on a 736-square-metre corner site in the heart of the Clifton Hill village and includes 29 rented rooms on the top floors. A gin distillery currently occupies some of the space and operates the bottleshop, but the pub is ripe for a new publican prepared to revamp the historic site.



Neighbours were outraged in 2019 when the Gudics lodged a bid for a residential project above the once-loved but shuttered pub in the enclave east of Hoddle Street. Colliers agents Ben Baines and Lucas Soccio are running the September 10 auction campaign and expect a price in the mid-$5 million range. Related Article City life Spawned from inner-city muck, this suburb full of lawyers is getting younger “There’s nothing better than a corner hotel in a village setting,” Baines said. Records show the Gudic family bought the pub in 1985 from Carlton & United Breweries with “5000 class 52 redeemable preference shares”. If that sounds like a complex way to buy a pub, it’s worth remembering CUB was taken over by Elders IXL in 1983 during the heady “corporate raider” period of management heralded by the late John Elliot.



Stingo Down Hoddle Street into Collingwood, investor Joe Awad has snapped up the Yorkshire Stingo Hotel for $2.5 million, a deal which reflects a skinny 3.82 per cent yield. The City East Motel behind it fetched $3.5 million. It’s not quite the total $8 million result that was hoped for the two properties. The pub, at 40-48 Hoddle Street, and the motel, at 181 Langridge Street, were bought by the Freeman family in 1988 for $130,000. The Yorkshire Stingo, on the corner of Hoddle and Langridge streets. Both properties cover 1136 square metres of land and were earmarked for a development along with another 1121 square metres at the rear. Those three warehouses, at 197-203 Landgridge Street, were owned by Munro Shoes – one of the last remaining shoe manufacturers in Abbotsford – and sold for $3 million. Stonebridge’s Max Warren, Dylan Kilner, Nic Hage and Chao Zhang handled negotiations.



Chinatown Last month’s hot auction in Chinatown, where 172-176 Little Bourke Street sold for $6.11 million, has inspired a clutch of owners to test the market with their own long-held properties. First up is 179 Russell Street, which is going to auction on August 26. The 180-square-metre two-level building is on a 102-square-metre piece of the city and is expected to fetch more than $3 million. It’s got a new lease and fitout to Jin Noodle Restaurant, which pays $165,000 a year in rent. 179 Russell Street, in Melbourne’s Chinatown district. Records show it last sold in 1994 for $1.05 million. Savills agents Julian Heatherich and Tom O’Halloran, with the Di Petta Group’s Winnie Chow, are running the auction campaign.



On August 27, the loveliest of the lot, 107 Little Bourke Street goes under the hammer. Designed by one of Melbourne’s best architects, Nahum Barnett, in 1903, the three-storey building last changed hands in 1970 for $27,000. It’s on a 99-square-metre parcel of land and rented to Khao Soi Melbourne. Lemon Baxter’s Hans Fan expects it to sell for about $4.8 million, which equates to a yield of 4.1 per cent. 107 Little Bourke Street, in Melbourne’s Chinatown district. Next month, 218-220 Little Bourke Street will be up for auction after 70 years in the one family’s hands. The double-storey shop of 325 square metres is expected to sell for about $4 million on September 3.



The building has a 10-year lease, with a 10-year option to the Lost Bar, which pays just under $180,000 a year in rent. Records show a quarter-share in the building last changed hands in 2004 for $500,000 and in 1970, a half-stake was transferred for $32,000. Fitzroys’ Lewis Waddell, Ben Liu and David Bourke are running the auction. According to Fitzroys’ latest Walk the CBD report, Chinatown vacancies nearly halved in the past year to 3.5 per cent from 6.6 per cent. 218-220 Little Bourke Street, Melbourne. There are a clutch of cafes and restaurants for sale along the west end too but not at auction.



Brendan Sullivan is selling the freehold of the long-running Grain Store restaurant at 517 Flinders Lane. Sullivan has been progressively selling the office and retail complex on Flinders Lane, which he bought in 2011 from the Smorgon family for $16.35 million. CBRE’s Alex Brierley, Nathan Mufale and Jing Jun Heng have the listing and expect about $3 million. At 540 Little Collins Street, the freehold of the Five Points bagel outlet is also for sale and expected to sell for about $1 million through Fitzroys’ Waddell and Liu. The Grain Store at 517 Flinders Lane. Lemon Baxter’s Fans and Paul O’Sullivan are also selling the Jumbo Kebabs freehold at 200 Spencer Street, opposite Southern Cross Station. It has a $1.95 million price tag.



Sculptor The North Melbourne laneway studio of the renowned late sculptor Erwin Fabian is up for sale. Fabian, born in Berlin in 1915, travelled to Australia in the 1940s on the ship the Dunera after escaping Nazi Germany in 1938. He joined the Australian Army’s education unit during World War II before returning to London for 12 years. He came back to Australia as a sculptor working with found pieces of metal. Inside the North Melbourne studio of sculptor Erwin Fabian. Fabian, whose work was described as “conceptual illusionism” by art professor Sasha Grishin, died in 2020.



The studio of 117 square metres is off Arden Street at 3-5 Wylies Lane, in the central pocket between Curzon and Errol streets. It’s on 152 square metres of land and goes to auction on August 27. Simpsons agents Richard Simpson and Ariana McCarron expect between $900,000 and $990,000 for the property. “Artwork not included” is the disappointing postscript to the Simpsons ad. Armadale redux Armadale’s blue-chip High Street has another large property up for sale, a 1990s office building halfway between Glenferrie and Kooyong roads. Records show the vendors of 1113-1121 High Street paid $3.45 million in 1996 and are looking at a payday of about $13.5 million.



113-1121 High Street, Armadale The 1589-square-metre building has five shops at street level, four offices upstairs and 61 car spaces. It’s on a large site of 1363 square metres. It has three agents on the case: Cushman & Wakefield’s Oliver Hay, Maker Property’s George Davies and Gross Waddell ICR’s Alex Ham. Last week, 935-951 High Street, on 1373 square metres, hit the market with a price tag of about $15.5 million and a permit for an apartment project.
