World.title: We think our boss has become obsessed with a chatbot. What can we do?
World.content:
BusinessWorkplaceWork therapy Opinion We think our boss has become obsessed with a chatbot. What can we do? Jonathan Rivett Careers contributor July 31, 2026 — 5:01am

July 31, 2026 — 5:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

I used to have a strong professional relationship with my boss and I respected them. But they have changed recently. Once they were considerate and supportive – some colleagues even thought they were a bit too gentle. Now they are neither of those things. They are definitely not gentle. They have started talking about instituting a new regime based on the advice of a friend and business mentor. All the new policies and ideas seem severe. A small group of people who report to this boss (including me) have talked in private about who this “mentor” is and why they are telling our manager to be so harsh and punishing. Our team is performing well, and has for years. There is now a strong rumour that the friend is actually an AI chatbot. Surely, that can’t be true, can it? There could be any number of reasons for how this has come about. John Shakespeare It certainly seems extraordinary that a professional could become so attached to a chatbot that they would change their entire work style and personality based on its “opinion”. Extraordinary but not inconceivable. About three years ago, a reader wrote to me about a work problem that they had reported to their HR team. They had been rudely brushed off. When they experimentally asked a chatbot about the same problem, the AI response was infinitely more empathetic and sensitive.



Although we can put this down to the tendency of modern large language model (LLM) chatbots to validate and endorse the concerns or ideas of its user, partly as a way of keeping the conversation going, an unflattering term like “AI sycophancy” doesn’t change the experience of that reader. Or anyone who speaks with AI and finds “someone” who appears to genuinely listen. I’m not going to say I know for sure what is going on with your boss. They may not be consulting a chatbot at all (although I find the evidence proposed in your longer email, via your worried colleagues, compelling). But to answer your direct question: yes, it can absolutely be true. People today are anthropomorphising AI in all sorts of different ways – this is no longer a fringe practice. Some people develop what are known as parasocial relationships with this new generation of ultra-coherent AI models. “Parasocial interaction” is a term coined in the 1950s to describe, for example, the way a TV viewer might come to think of a media personality as their friend, despite the relationship being entirely one-way. Now, some experts in the field believe “parasocial” is not quite the right term to apply to profound relationships between humans and AI. Whereas in the ’50s a TV presenter might inadvertently (or at least perfunctorily) encourage parasocial intimacy by looking down the camera and talking directly to the audience, in the 2020s a chatbot mimics interest, understanding and even love in a highly sophisticated, often utterly earnest, way.



Let’s stick with the term for now, at any rate. Editor's pick Opinion

Work therapy My colleague is constantly negative. How can I make them cheer up? Jonathan Rivett Careers contributor We know that people today are anthropomorphising AI in all sorts of different ways – this is no longer a fringe practice. They converse with their favourite chatbot as they might a human therapist, a companion, a “troubleshooter” and even a “work buddy”. If your boss is doing that, but has entered into a pathological version of parasocial engagement, it’s quite possible that they’re taking advice from this digital confidant in good faith, genuinely understanding it to be their intimate. And perhaps their teller of cold, hard truths. There could be any number of reasons for how this has come about. It might have been a conversational chain reaction, beginning with a benign question but branching, exchange by exchange, into something much more radical.



Or it may have been less accidental. Perhaps your boss, worried that they were seen as a soft touch, sought advice on changing this perception, and were given a menu of aggressive and ruthless management tactics. The change won’t have come out of nowhere. And while I think it’s sensible to be curious about, and even sympathetic to, what catalysed it, you don’t need to tolerate or excuse the cold-hearted turn. Your manager, of course, has the prerogative to make changes, and is under no obligation to be your friend, but if they’re taking dogmatic advice from a chatbot, I think they’re engaging in an ill-advised, even dangerous practice – and possibly stepping onto legally shaky ground. One day in the future consulting with robots as if they’re trustworthy humans might be entirely normal, and possibly beneficial. That day has not arrived. Send your questions through to Work Therapy by emailing jonathan@theinkbureau.com.au Get workplace news, advice and perspectives to help make your job work for you.

World.title: Priscilla’s pub to get a $5 million facelift by its new operator
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesCommercial real estate Priscilla’s pub to get a $5 million facelift by its new operator Carolyn Cummins July 31, 2026 — 5:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Capital Gain The Imperial Erskineville, in Sydney’s inner west – one of the venues featured in the film The Adventures of Priscilla, Queen of the Desert – is getting a facelift to take the venue into its next phase. Odd Culture Group is the new operator and will work with the owners, Universal Hotels, to give the “Impy”, as it is affectionately known, a $5 million renovation that will see its ground floor double in size, through an expanded beer garden as well as a 24-hour basement bar. The Imperial Erskineville is getting a major makeover. James Brickwood Universal Hotels acquired the Impy in 2023 for about $20 million from The Sydney Collective’s Fraser Short and Australian Hotels Association NSW President Scott Leach who saved the site from closure in 2015.



Constructed in 1880, the Impy at 35 Erskineville Road, has been an institution and symbol of the queer community over many years of its operations. Last year, the venue was also added to the NSW State Heritage Register for its “deep cultural and historical significance”. Editor's pick Commercial real estate Will it be third try lucky for controversial car park in exclusive Double Bay? Odd Culture, known for its portfolio of inclusive and diverse venues across Sydney, is an operator of other Universal Hotels’ venues, including the Universal, The Oxford and The Riley pubs, and is run by founder and chief executive James Thorpe. He said the aim of the renovations is to secure both groups’ “long-term investment in the future of queer nightlife and artistic expression in Sydney”. “The Imperial has spent more than 40 years helping to shape Sydney’s queer culture. This redevelopment is one of the biggest investments in its history, but more importantly, it’s an investment in the next 40 years,” Thorpe said.



It’s business as usual at the Impy with Odd Culture taking the reins from September 1, with the renovations slated to start in early 2027. Arnaout’s Wisemans Inn Fresh from his $500 million sale of seven regional pubs, Iris Capital’s Sam Arnaout is selling his Wisemans Inn Hotel on the banks of the Hawkesbury River, north-west of Sydney. The Wisemans Inn Hotel. Arnaout bought the 195-year-old pub in September 2022 from Bill Young for about $10 million and is divesting it as part of his plan to focus on Sydney-based projects.



The pub opened in 1827 on a 5123-square-metre landholding and includes accommodation comprising six freestanding motel suites and five boutique pub rooms. The venue generates about $3.2 million in annual turnover. It is close to a new boat ramp with 163 bays, but there is potential for expanded al fresco dining, family-friendly spaces, and special events programming. JLL Hotels & Hospitality Group agents Kate MacDonald, Greg Jeloudev and Ben McDonald are advising on the sale. Seven Hills The former Mercedes-Benz processing and parts storage centre in Seven Hills is being sold by the private vendor SHMPC Pty Limited with price expectations of $25 million to $27 million. Constructed in 2018, the 29 Brumby Street site is being offered with vacant possession in the short term and comprises 5408 sq m of office and warehouse facilities on a 9703 sq m general industrial landholding and sits in the Blacktown City Council zone.



The property currently generates net rental income of about $1.46 million per annum. It is purpose-built for vehicle-intensive operations and comes with a 100kW solar system. Colliers’ Paul McGlynn is advising on the sale. 29 Brumby Street, Seven Hills. NRL hotel With the tom-toms beating in the jungle that the National Rugby League is scouting Sydney for a new hotel, the hospitality sector is proving a happy hunting ground for investors and owners. While no details have emerged, the Australian Rugby League Commission chairman Peter V’landys said recently that the NRL was looking to boost its property empire to be worth about $1 billion.



It has been suggested the NRL is looking at the Novotel Sydney International Airport hotel based in Wolli Creek. If the deal is done, it will add to its existing portfolio in Sydney which includes the Quest Woolooware Bay. It also owns the ibis Styles Port Macquarie hotel. The potential sale comes as hotels continue to scoop up property awards. Last month, the Surry Hills Village by TOGA which includes the Eve Hotel won the Urban Taskforce Australia’s 2026 Development of the Year. At the Accommodation Australia NSW Awards for Excellence held last week, the Luxury Hotel of the Year award was won by Park Hyatt Sydney, while the Metropolitan Deluxe Hotel of the Year went to Sheraton Grand Sydney Hyde Park. carolynannecummins@gmail.com The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. World.title: The Melbourne intersection that epitomises where our road safety approach is going wrong
World.content:
We live in Melbourne’s inner west. I drive a hatchback, but commute by bike. Our son has been learning to drive for the last year. Recently, turning right at a quiet intersection, he panicked. There was no hazard; just traffic lights without a right-turn arrow. In a year of supervised driving, our ultra-controlled road system had so thoroughly insulated him that he’d never been required to exercise his own judgment in this everyday scenario.

As a professional designer, this was a red flag. In my industry, we practise user-centred design in which we distil and design for the user’s core purpose, and minimise any factors that impede this. The core purpose of any road system is to move from A to B as safely, economically and efficiently as possible. But Victoria’s “Safe System” framework has abandoned this balance. Physical and prescriptive impediments to our road system’s core function are being rolled out without restraint. More frustratingly, we’re being asked to endure a lot of usability pain for almost no safety gain.

Peak compliance: The Macaulay Road level crossing in Kensington has more than 10 different signs competing for attention. Steve Martinuzzo

In design, it’s a failure if the core function of a system is compromised by other objectives. If I designed a medical device that was totally safe but didn’t work, I’d be out of a job. Yet, by trying to micro-control everything, this is exactly what our road authorities are doing. And by treating the human driver as a liability rather than an accountable citizen, our roads and policies are becoming increasingly incongruent to the community they should support.

Good information design relies on visual hierarchy, which means telling the user just what they need to know at the moment they need to know it. No less, and definitely no more. However, today’s roads break every rule of visual information design.

World.title: Mystery death of the original ‘gymfluencer’: Inside the tragic final days of Zyzz
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

You can’t miss Aziz “Zyzz” Shavershian’s headstone in a grassy corner of Riverstone cemetery in Sydney’s north-west. There he is, looking back at you from an oval ceramic photo set in the granite, a muscular bicep straining against the fabric of his tight black T-shirt, all tousled, gelled hair and coal-black eyes, against an image of a tranquil ocean meeting an endless blue summer sky. Etched beneath the dates of his short life – March 24, 1989 to August 5, 2011 – is Zyzz’s signature mantra, Veni, Vidi, Vici (“I came, I saw, I conquered”) that in life was tattooed across his hairless, sculpted chest. Over the years, a steady stream of local and overseas fans have made the pilgrimage here, to lay flowers and cards on the polished granite base under the gum trees, or post videos on commemorative pages on Instagram, YouTube and Facebook (one such page has 346,000 followers). Many of the tributes left on these digital shrines are overwhelmingly effusive. “Thank you for changing mine and a million other lives,” a visitor from Seattle posted on Instagram. “After 12 years, I finally made it to your grave. It was an honour to pay my respects,” declared a muscly, tattooed compatriot on Instagram. “You motivated me to get off the couch and get to the gym,” gushed one Australian man on YouTube. Back in 2010 and 2011, before TikTok and Snapchat, before Instagram became popular, and before the reign of the insidious algorithms that would turn social media into an endless echo-chamber, Zyzz racked up hundreds of thousands of views for his videos on YouTube and a loyal follower base on bodybuilding forums and his Facebook page. Aziz “Zyzz’ Shavershian at his gym in Sydney’s Carlingford at age 19. @zyzz_page_official/Instagram A skinny, shy World of Warcraft gamester and star high-school student who metamorphosed into a muscly party boy, Aziz brought the classic nerd-to-superman archetype to life through Zyzz, baiting his legion of young male followers to “get aesthetic” in videos shot from his bedroom webcam or by members of his crew while he was partying or sweating it out in the gym. The videos were always amateurish, often fun, sometimes cringeworthy, occasionally offensive, but they resonated. After his death, Zyzz became more popular and mythologised than he ever was in life. By the standards of today’s vast army of bulked-up online gym influencers (“gymfluencers”) – the top tier of whom can earn in the millions – Zyzz was as lean as a lamp post, but that was precisely his bedrock appeal. Because his transformation from teen beanpole to sculpted Adonis didn’t shout steroid-bolstered size (even though he did use image-enhancing drugs), his muscle growth at least seemed plausible – albeit one attributable to a mighty amount of grit, hard work and self-discipline. Which is why his signature mantra, “We’re all gonna make it, brahs,” became a rallying cry. Some credit Zyzz and his “aesthetics crew”, which included his older brother, Said Shavershian, who adopted the name of Chestbrah, with upending the world of bodybuilding, shifting the focus away from sheer size and thickness to a tight, V-shaped physique. “At that time, bodybuilding was still a cult sport that only attracted guys with superior genetics and a desire to put on bulk,” recalls Said, who is now 40 and runs a successful online training business supported by more than 437,000 followers on Instagram. “We changed the game by showing people that you don’t need to be an overblown bodybuilder to look good. Most men dream of having a physique like Brad Pitt in Troy or Zac Efron in Baywatch, but not every man wants to look like Arnold Schwarzenegger.”



As Zyzz’s online star rose, so did the online backlash from trolls calling him a wanker, a gym douche, and a “fake natty” (someone who is using steroids but pretends to be natural). And not surprisingly, given he invited fans and haters alike to admire his physique (“You mirin’ brah?“), he also became a magnet for competitive hostility from other men – and, sometimes, outright aggression. On one occasion, according to his brother, he was set upon by a bunch of hoons outside a nightclub; he briefly fended them off and jumped into a passing taxi, but before the vehicle sped away, his attackers shoved their arms through the window and tried to wrench him out. While he publicly dismissed the vitriol with bravado – “I’d rather be a person that’s hated on, than a person that does the hating” – there were signs that the deeply vulnerable young man was increasingly undone by it. For a man obsessed with his appearance, the cruel attacks on his facial features, most notably his prominent nose, must have particularly stung. Related Article Good Weekend Elijah was 10 when his friend typed ‘porn’ into a search engine. He was afraid – but unable to look away The relentless demand for more and better content, combined with a lifestyle of nightclubs, music festivals and heavy training – all fuelled by a volatile cocktail of steroids, recreational drugs and Xanax – began to take its toll, leaving Aziz utterly exhausted by his own alter-ego creation within just 18 months or so. “There is no ‘Zyzz’, that is just an act,” he posted in a revealing video in the months before his death. When news broke in August 2011 that the 22-year-old internet phenomenon had died in Thailand – reportedly in a sauna, from a previously undiagnosed heart condition – public speculation ran wild. Was the cardiac arrest caused by steroid use, recreational drugs in the sauna or an underlying, unmanaged heart condition? Some days later, when it was revealed that a thief had stolen belongings from Aziz’s hotel room – including his laptop, wallet and clothes – conspiracy theories flourished. Behind the tragic headlines, the truth never entirely came out. Now, as the 15th anniversary of Aziz’s death approaches, a new documentary to be aired from August 5 on Stan (owned by Nine Entertainment, the owners of this masthead) explores the rise of the self-proclaimed “son of Zeus and brother of Hercules”. Poster Boy: Becoming Zyzz contains some dramatic new information about his death (we’ll get to this a bit later), including his real reason for going to Thailand, and some morbidly compelling medical details about what killed him.



Aziz and Said Shavershian probably would not have made it to Australia had it not been for the collapse of the Soviet Union in the early 1990s and the elder brother’s severe childhood asthma. Having lost most of their assets in the upheaval and seeking a warmer, drier climate for Said’s condition, the boys’ Russian-Kurdish parents, both of whom were doctors in Moscow, moved to Australia in 1993, when Said was seven and Aziz four, finally settling in Sydney’s Carlingford, a family-friendly, middle-class area in the city’s north-west. Theirs was the classic migrant tale of starting afresh and building a new life which, for the parents, meant getting their degrees again. They had high hopes for their sons, wanting them to be doctors or lawyers, but fortune took them in another direction. Both brothers had lingering lisps when they were small; unable to pronounce Aziz, older brother Said called him “Zyzz” and the nickname stuck. At Marist College in Eastwood, an all-boys Catholic school, the brothers were as academically impressive as they were athletically unassuming, with Aziz distinguishing himself as the school’s dux. The boys grew up watching WWE – their heroes were Hulk Hogan and Ultimate Warrior – and geeked out over games like Warcraft. As the high school years advanced, the professional hopes of the parents took a back seat as the boys found a physical outlet in the gym. “I started bodybuilding because I was bullied a bit in school for being so skinny,” Said tells Good Weekend. “So I wanted to build a bit of muscle mass to look intimidating to other men, and also get the attention of girls.” Aziz soon followed his brother to the gym and found his natural home there. “He started getting bigger than me, and I didn’t know why,” Said told Neil “The Muscle” Cummins, a former Kings Cross bouncer, in a frank interview last year for Cummins’ Secrets of the Underworld podcast. “And then I walked in on him putting a needle in his bum. And I’m like, ‘You little f-----, you’ve been doing this behind my back.’ “Around year 11, he started learning about girls and drugs, and it went downhill from there,” Said also told Cummins. “He was very hard to control. Even my parents couldn’t control him.” Phillip Raymond, who became a friend of Aziz during this time, trained with him at Fitness First in Carlingford, and also filmed content for his videos. He says Aziz had charisma in spades. “Girls wanted to be with him and guys wanted to hang out with him,” he recalls. What didn’t come across in his boisterous videos was Aziz’s intelligence. “He was super-intelligent, very switched on.” Loading



Given that Aziz, at 185 centimetres tall and super skinny, had the type of frame that in gym parlance is a “hard-gainer”, his transformation, via high-volume, heavy resistance training, would have taken years without chemical enhancement. Phillip Raymond explains that he never had to resort to steroids because, with a shorter (he’s 170 centimetres), thicker, mesomorphic physique, he has always been able to pack on muscle quickly. But Aziz was a young man in a hurry – he wanted the dream physique and appeared to relish the image of the hypermasculine alpha male that can accompany it, even if it was just that: an image. “You lift weights, you get tatts, you f--- bitches, brah,” he once crudely boasted to his fans in a video. Selina Miles, director of Poster Boy, whose award-winning documentary Silenced focused on the fight against laws silencing sexual-abuse survivors, told Good Weekend she was determined not to skate over Zyzz’s at times boorish braggadocio. “I couldn’t promise participants we wouldn’t be looking at that,” she says. “By the same token, it’s really important for audiences to remember he was 20 when he became famous and only 22 when he died. When you meet his friends, you think, ‘This guy must have been all right.’ Many of the people who loved him have grown into really self-aware, considerate men.” For years after Aziz’s death, Said was forced to be a reluctant apologist for his brother’s often distasteful stunts and statements, such as when Zyzz wore his T-shirt as a turban and mockingly mimicked prayer. Aziz was just being a “clown”, a “dickhead” under his Zyzz persona, Said told Neil Cummins. Said insisted that those alter-ego antics did not reflect his brother’s real-life views, that he had a diverse group of mates, including Muslims and gay friends. And despite his reputation as a playboy, which was “partly true”, Aziz had a steady girlfriend for three years. Over the past 15 years, Said has put considerable energy into preserving his younger brother’s name and complex legacy, most notably by producing a 19-minute YouTube video (Zyzz: The Legacy) that has attracted more than 18 million views. So in 2022, when documentary producer Tom Blackwell approached Said about making a documentary looking at Zyzz’s life, he pounced at the opportunity. “There’s a bit of Zyzz in all of us,” Aziz once declared. Said Shavershian, who is now 40, is intent on preserving his younger brother’s legacy. James Brickwood If anything, Aziz’s short life and his Zyzz persona serves as a mirror for a look-at-me selfie culture that has only grown exponentially more pervasive since his passing, reaching a new inflection point with the current phenomenon of “looksmaxxing”. (Said has been upfront on Instagram about his own enhancements: “Hair transplant: $10,000; Veneers $15,000; “Brotox” $500 for six months; Supps and TRT [testosterone replacement therapy], $500 per month.“) But the “looksmaxxing” terrain becomes very dubious – and dangerous – in extreme examples led by influencers such as Clavicular, who advocate bone injury and smashing to create a more chiselled jawline and cheekbones (there is no medical evidence backing these methods).



Daniel Principe, a high-profile youth advocate best known for his campaigns to promote healthy masculinity, was a little younger than Aziz when the Zyzz persona was riding high. “We all love a transformation story and Zyzz had an appeal, especially for guys who weren’t particularly sporty, jockish, or ladsy – he told us, ‘You, too, could achieve the ultimate physique,’” Principe recalls. “At the time, no one else was putting themselves out there like him. Now it’s a saturated market, with both the number of gym bros and fitness influencers.” It certainly looks that way: back in 2010, when Zyzz was pumping out sets on the bench-press at Fitness First in Carlingford, there were 800 gyms and fitness centres in Australia; today, there are more than 7300. For young men in particular, anything that drags them away from their screens has to be a good thing. Yet, Principe is disturbed by the sheer volume of “fitfluencers”, biohackers and celebrities who are injecting steroids and peptides to maintain a perfect body, while insisting to their followers they have achieved their results by hard training, diet and over-the-counter supplements. ‘Perhaps even the supplement sponsors don’t really care if an influencer is hiding their steroid use.’ Youth advocate Daniel Principe “Even if a young man suspects an influencer is on steroids, he can’t escape the visual saturation of images of ‘giga chads’ – idealised versions of alpha males – confronting him daily on platforms like TikTok and Instagram,” says Principe. “Perhaps even the supplement sponsors don’t really care if an influencer is hiding their steroid use because it’s like, ‘You’re helping me sell my product, so who cares?’ ” Related Article Good Weekend ‘What’s bubbling underneath’: Showing teen boys how to master emotion and empathy No generation in human history has spent more time watching, listening and interacting with their peers – and less time listening to their parents and older mentors – than people under 25 today, thanks to social media invading every corner of our lives, Principe points out. This makes the battle for parents, and mentors with wiser heads, more challenging than ever, he says. The underlying driver of all this self-obsession is something far more insidious than narcissism in the classical sense, according to research over the past few years: it’s constant body surveillance, fuelled by looking at social media feeds for hours every day. Far from motivating us to improve our lives – get out and exercise, eat healthily – we’re often left feeling anxious, inadequate and confused by the flood of images.

World.title: South Island set for first direct international internet cable
World.content:
Southland and Australia look set to be linked by the first international submarine cable to land in New Zealand's South Island, as plans advance for a massive data centre in the region.

Singapore-owned Datagrid New Zealand said it had signed contracts for the supply and installation of the cable with Alcatel Submarine Networks and OMS Group.

The agreement covers a new 2300-kilometre submarine cable between Invercargill and Melbourne, forming part of Datagrid's wider Tasman Ring Network project.

Datagrid's Tasman Ring Network is expected to eventually connect the North and South islands with Sydney and Melbourne, spanning about 6000km.

Datagrid chief executive Rémi Galasso said the connection would be a "game changer" for Southland and the South Island.

"It will unlock the potential of the region, and will allow South Island IT companies, universities and research centres to benefit from better internet with latency improved by up to 45 percent compared with existing routes via the North Island."

Datagrid chief executive Rémi Galasso (L) and Mercury chief executive Stewart Hamilton. Supplied / Datagrid NZ

The announcement dovetails with Datagrid's proposed hyperscale 280MW data centre at Makarewa, near Invercargill, which is expected to cost between NZ$3.3 billion and NZ$3.5b and become one of the largest data centre developments in New Zealand.

The Southland data centre has already secured resource consents, while the company is separately developing the Tasman Ring international cable network.

The project received a boost last week when Mercury announced it would invest NZ$53 million for a 12.7 percent stake in Datagrid NZ.

Once operational, the data centre would become one of New Zealand's largest electricity users, second only to the Tiwai Point aluminium smelter according to some estimates.

The project has attracted controversy over its expected electricity demand and water use, although Datagrid has argued the facility will support New Zealand's ambitions in artificial intelligence, cloud computing and digital infrastructure.

World.title: Is Australia losing its shine?
World.content:
What's good debt, what's bad debt and how do I tell the difference? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 11m

A promise of a better life in Australia has drawn many New Zealanders across the Tasman in recent years. But economists say the tide may be about to turn.

As the economy slowed after the post-Covid boom, the number of New Zealanders migrating to Australia picked up. There was a net migration loss of 28,500 people to Australia in the year to December last year, smaller than the 31,100 in 2024 but much higher than the 3000 a year that was normal between 2014 and 2019.

The record was a loss of 43,700 in the year to March 2012.

Simplicity chief economist Shamubeel Eaqub said people were drawn to Australia because the country was richer and had become steadily more so than New Zealand for the last 40 years.

Australia's GDP per person started to diverge from New Zealand's in the 1970s and is now significantly higher.

Eaqub said that was partly because of their commodity prices and a better terms of trade but it was not only mining that helped. New Zealanders were earning less on average and spending more of their income on housing.

But he said where New Zealand's house price relative to GDP per person, and rents relative to GDP had been higher for a long time, they were starting to converge.

"For a long time, New Zealand's housing market has just been really terrible in terms of how unaffordable it is, both in terms of house prices and rents… we spend a lot more of our income on housing compared to Australia, everything else is much the same.

"Ours has got a little bit better and theirs has got a lot worse."

Eaqub said the current slowdown in Australia's housing market could change the picture again but New Zealand had made more progress with its conversation about public policy and housing in recent years than Australia had.

"I'm not saying we're perfect but I think it's far more mature here than it is over there."

He said Australia's economy also had headwinds and unemployment rising, which might discourage people from moving there if their access to welfare was likely to be limited. Australia also has higher central bank interest rates with similar levels of inflation.

A comparison of house prices relative to GDP per capita in Australia and New Zealand from 1995 until 2025. Supplied / Simplicity

There was a net migration loss of 28,500 people to Australia in the year to December last year, Supplied / Qantas

BNZ chief economist Mike Jones agreed there were signs that "some of those economic relativities are starting to tilt more towards New Zealand".

"Probably more so from the Australian side as the Aussie economy slows down. Household spending growth there is entering a softer patch alongside falling house prices and a likely further rise in unemployment. As an example, New Zealand job ads have been, tentatively, rising against a flat-to-lower trend in Australia. That's historically quite a good indicator to suggest some narrowing in the big gap between New Zealand and Aussie unemployment rates is likely. That subtle shift in labour market relativities is I think one of the key reasons why New Zealand departures to Australia have slowed up a little."

He said he would still frame it more as New Zealand catching up rather than overtaking.

"Australia's economy starts from an outright stronger position in nearly all areas. Our forecasts do have New Zealand growth catching up and eventually overtaking that of Australia over the next 12-18 months, but it could be quite a while before New Zealand's unemployment rate falls down to where Australia's resides in the mid-to-late 4s."

ANZ senior economist Miles Workman said the two economies had been on different paths for a while.and New Zealand had more of a "boom-bust" Covid experience than Australia.

"That's likely to remain the case for a while yet, with New Zealand starting from a weaker position than Australia in terms of economic momentum, meaning the hurdle to growth in New Zealand should be a bit lower. The starting point for the respective housing markets is a similar story.

"The difference in unemployment rates between Australia and New Zealand helps explain the trans-Tasman migration cycle. Our forecasts have that gap narrowing from late this year, which should reduce some of the incentive to move purely for cyclical labour market reasons.

"However, it will take more than a few years of business cycle divergence to address the more structural income differential between the two countries. Even if New Zealand's economy outperforms Australia's for a period, skilled workers will likely still be able to earn materially more in Australia doing similar work. Australia's labour market is also larger, with more major cities, industries and career opportunities to choose from."

He said it was possible New Zealand would start to look more attractive over the next little while, because it was coming off a weaker base.

"Closing the gap with Australia in a more structural sense would require stronger productivity growth over the long run, which is what ultimately drives higher incomes. A cyclical upswing alone is unlikely to be enough."

Westpac senior economist Satish Ranchhod last year argued that New Zealand's economic growth was likely to outpace Australia's.

World.title: Water bills in Auckland and Wellington to climb as investment is made in infrastructure
World.content:
Water bills in Auckland and Wellington are about to climb, as water companies try to catch up on decades of under-investment.

In Auckland, Watercare revealed on Thursday an average household's water bill would go up about $8 per month, as part of a $15.2 billion investment in the city's water infrastructure.

Meanwhile in Wellington, people would pay 13.3 percent more as new water agency Tiaki Wai invested in ageing infrastructure.

A wastewater leak in Wellington's CBD in October 2024. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

Auckland has been plagued by problems with its ageing water infrastructure, including in 2023 when a huge sinkhole in Parnell meant millions of litres of sewage a day were pumped into the Waitemata harbour.

Deputy Mayor Desley Simpson said Watercare's $15b investment would prevent those kind of problems in the future.

"It means that we're going to get investment that we've been crying out for ages, below the ground to improve water quality... and actually finally gets us an Auckland that we can swim at our beaches with no black flags."

Auckland Deputy Mayor Desley Simpson. RNZ / Nick Monro

Separating Watercare from Auckland Council, with its own balance sheet, had meant it could take on more debt to fund the infrastructure, Simpson said.

Watercare has also put up water prices, by about $8 per month for the average Auckland household, to help pay for it.

"And that's painful. It's a tough economic time. But I suppose one of the advantages we have in Auckland is we can, as households, monitor how much we spend. You know, if you have shorter showers," Simpson said.

Aucklanders RNZ spoke to agreed the increase would be painful.

"Well it affects everyone doesn't it? To a degree. I think I could afford $8, but a lot of people can't," said one.

"For lower-income people, it probably would be a challenge for them, so I feel sorry for them in that regard," said another.

But many felt the extra cost was worth it, if it meant fewer issues with the water network in the future.

"I sometimes go to Mission Bay and you can't swim there because there's some warning sign saying that it's contaminated. So I definitely look forward to that."

"It's heartbreaking really, we're supposed to be this clean, green country and summer after summer not being able to go to the beach."

A sign warns of a sewage leak at an Auckland beach. RNZ / Nikki Mandow

In Wellington, council organisation Tiaki Wai has taken over management of water services, and sent out its first new bills on Wednesday.

Water bills in the city would increase by 13.3 percent on average this year.

Wellingtonian Charlotte Murphy felt there hadn't been enough communication that the new bills were coming.

"I haven't seen a lot of information as a ratepayer about it, and I know that there are a lot of questions around it from people in, for example, my apartment complex."

Back in Auckland, Watercare chief executive Jamie Sinclair told Checkpoint the infrastructure work it was doing was urgently needed.

"We've got significant underinvestment in the assets that we own. The 20,000 kilometres of pipe or so that we maintain at the moment. We also need to build resilence into our network as we're dealing with more extreme weather events and also increasing demand."

World.title: 'Doesn't hurt so much now': Kiwi cyclist recovers from crash to win gold
World.content:
It's a full set of medals for New Zealand on the first day of track cycling at the Commonwealth Games with a gold, a silver and two bronze medals.

Paracyclist Emma Foy and pilot Jessie Hodges won gold in the women's tandem B sprint final.

Australia won the first race in the best of three final, but a collision between the two in the second race delayed the event.

Foy and Hodges then picked themselves up to win race two and dominated race three in a performance Foy was proud of.

"It was what we were planning to do before the crash and we practised these sort of things at training and we were able to pull it off," Foy said.

Hodges said the crash didn't affect them too much.

"We were definitely sore but we were just saying after the gold it doesn't hurt so much now.

"It makes all the training and the blood, sweat and tears all worth it."

Foy is a former world champion on both the road and the track.

The women's pursuit team couldn't compete with Australia in the 4000m final with the defending champions recording a games record time, with New Zealand finishing two seconds behind them.

"We wanted to get the gold for sure but I think we can be super proud of the silver. We strive to do the best we can and I think we did that out there today," said team member Bryony Botha.

Nicole Murray rode a world record time to grab the bronze medal in the women's C4-C5 4000m individual pursuit. The time was later eclipsed by Australian Tara Neyland in the gold medal ride.

The men's pursuit team beat Wales in the bronze medal ride, while Australia beat England for gold.

There was disappointment for New Zealand in the women's team sprint with Ellesse Andrews, Olivia King and Rebecca Petch only managing the fifth fastest time and missing out on the medal rides.

World.title: Solar recommendations could speed up installations, lower household bills - industry
World.content:
New recommendations for solar power could speed up installations and lower household bills, the industry says.

Minister for Regulation David Seymour laid out 15 recommendations to streamline solar uptake in a review published on Thursday.

He also advised legalising plug-in solar, which is currently illegal in the country due to concerns over electricity and fire risks.

"You may have heard people say in Australia you can go to Kmart, buy a plug-in solar panel, plug it in and be going just as though you'd bought a PS2 or a Sega Megastation, or any other device for that matter.

"However, this is much better for the environment and you actually make money instead of wasting your childhood," said Seymour.

Electrification advocates Rewiring Aotearoa welcomed the recommendations.

Its policy director Dave Karl said the suggestions addressed the challenges stopping households from taking up solar: delays and unnecessary added costs.

"I think absolutely solar's day has come in New Zealand and I think the commitments from almost every party around the finance through the ratepayers assistance scheme, will absolutely unlock the choice for more than 90 percent of households to get solar on board."

Rewiring Aotearoa policy director Dave Karl. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

He said the review cut through red tape without sacrificing safety: accredited installers employing properly certified electricians would still be required.

"I do see it as a job creation opportunity in the medium to long run, and I really hope some parties come out with good policies around building that workforce domestically," he said.

He said legalising plug-in solar would make it very popular with renters.

"And I think more so than just plug-in solar, we'll be seeing lots of people also pairing that with plug-in batteries, enabling them to capture cheap electricity overnight and use that a little bit during the day as well.

"So I think it'll be, I mean, not as game-changing for power bills as rooftop solar can be, but shaving 50 bucks, 20 bucks - everything counts these days for a lot of families."

Future Energy co-founder Heath Coleman agreed this was a positive direction for the industry.

"I think we're all very supportive to see the removal, making solar easier and faster for homeowners to get solar, ultimately, at the end of the day," he said.

But he said the biggest challenge was the workforce.

"What we're facing at the moment is that there's a long process to get registered and solar installers to have the micro credentials that they need in order to sign off and install a solar system."

A home powered by solar. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

He said apprentices in his team of 80 would have to wait an extended period of time after their qualifications before being allowed to install solar.

"We're really struggling to find people that have the right skill sets there because it's still a very new and emerging industry. So, we have to train people up constantly and that takes time and obviously a lot of cost in there as well."

He said he wanted to see the certification process speed up.

However, he said he thought the upfront costs would still be a major deterrent - even with rate payers assistance schemes announced by several political parties.

"I think financially all the numbers do tend to stack up'" he said.

'Significant savings'

But Consumer NZ's power switch manager Paul Fuge said solar installations typically took less than a decade to pay themselves back.

"The other way to look at it is in terms of the unit price.

"So currently the average price in New Zealand is around 35 cents to 40 cents a kWh, depending on where you live. And solar is coming in around 15 cents, including the cost of capital.

"So there's significant savings in terms of the cost of the electricity that's coming off a solar system compared to buying it from the grid."

Consumer NZ' power switchmanager Paul Fuge. Supplied / Consumer NZ

The consumer champion said the perceived hassle and expense of solar deterred consumers.

"I mean, this review is really about removing unnecessary barriers. And if these reforms make solar quicker and easier to install without compromising safety, that's a win for consumers," he said.

He also welcomed legalising plug-in solar, as renters would be able to reap the benefits too.

"But what we'd say is installation is only half the story," he warned.

Fuge said he wanted to see more oversight of buy-back rates - the price of selling electricity back to the grid.

"Consumers also need to get fair pricing and fair returns from the electricity they generate from their solar systems."

James Scott from Electrify the Hutt, a community-led initiative to promote electrification, said allowing solar panel companies to sign off on an installation without an inspection would help speed up the process, but there was also a need for more installers to meet the demand.

The Ministry for Regulation said a small-scale solar system could involve up to six different sign-offs and five site visits from four different entities before it could be switched on.

James Scott from Electrify the Hutt. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Scott said his daughter and son-in-law had to wait around seven weeks due to the amount of red tape.

However, Scott added that he was able to be connected within 48 hours as his installer had done the preparatory work.

"I think that the regulatory review is one part of it, and taking away some of those things will help," he said.

"I think the other thing... is we need a good supply of trained and competent installers who know what they're doing."

Scott said some solar panel companies had more business than they could cope with.

World.title: FMA delivers offset loan warning for banks
World.content:
New Zealand's financial regulator is warning banks that offer offset mortgages to take notice of action in Australia.

The Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC) said its review had found customers might have been unknowingly paying more interest than they should because some banks had failed to properly manage offset accounts.

ASIC reviewed the offset practices of eight banks, representing more than 70 percent of Australia's A$2.5 trillion home loan market.

What's good debt, what's bad debt and how do I tell the difference? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 11m

It said, while practices varied significantly across the banks, it found weaknesses in how all banks set up, monitored and managed offset accounts, resulting in some customers missing out on promised savings.

Australian banks are the parent companies of Westpac, ANZ, ASB and BNZ.

Michael Hewes, director of deposit taking, insurance, advice and credit at the Financial Markets Authority, said it was encouraging banks in New Zealand offering offset products to consider ASIC's findings and reflect on the robustness of their controls to prevent similar harms impacting their customers.

"The Conduct of Financial Institutions regime requires Financial Institutions, including banks, to treat customers fairly and have effective policies, processes, systems and controls in place to do so. Additionally, the Credit Contracts and Consumer Finance Act requires lenders to provide clear disclosure of loan terms and to charge reasonable fees and interest.

"Our monitoring of financial institutions includes looking at the products they offer. One of our current regulatory priorities is focused on product design, ensuring that, when developing new products or redesigning existing ones, financial institutions prioritise consumer needs while also considering the capabilities and limitations of their systems and processes.

"This follows thematic monitoring we undertook last year which highlighted the risks posed by legacy systems and a reliance on manual controls."

He said the FMA had previously taken action when financial institutions had failed to deliver products as promised.

World.title: Labour considered most capable of managing New Zealanders' top five concerns - survey
World.content:
The Labour party is considered most capable of managing all of the top five concerns for New Zealanders - including the economy, the latest Ipsos Issues Monitor has revealed.

National leads on just one of the top 20 issues: crime/law and order.

The quarterly survey asks 1000 New Zealanders what they think are the three most important issues facing the country, and the political parties they believe are most capable of handling them.

The monitor showed New Zealanders' assessment of government performance remained low, with an average rating of 4.1 out of 10 (compared to 4.2 in May).

Less than a quarter of respondents rated the government's performance positively (that is, between 7-10 out of 10) compared to 27 percent in May.

Rating of government performance over six months. Supplied / Ipsos Issues Monitor

The top five issues

The cost of living (62 percent) remained the top concern since May's survey, and healthcare/hospitals (38 percent) was still considered second most important, though it's been slowly trending downwards.

National's perceived ability to manage healthcare weakened significantly, reaching its lowest point since February 2024, while Labour's at its highest level in nearly five years.

The economy (34 percent) held at third place, but Labour overtook National as the party best placed to manage it - spiking from 28 percent in May to 34 percent in July, while National dropped from 33 percent to 30 percent.

The political parties seen as most capable of managing issues. Supplied / Ipsos Issues Monitor

Labour also took a decent lead in the perception of its ability to tackle housing (22 percent) - ranked the fourth most important issue.

Unemployment (20 percent) returned to the top five concerns, reaching a level last seen in late 2020 and overtaking concerns about petrol prices.

The report said it surveyed people during the announced ceasefire in the US-Iran conflict, which drove a sharp decline in concern about fuel, dropping it from the fourth most important issue to seventh equal.

Other trends

Labour is considered best placed to tackle 15 of the top 20 issues.

The political parties seen as most capable of managing other issues. Supplied / Ipsos Issues Monitor

The Greens are most trusted with climate change as well as environmental concerns, National with law and order, and Te Pāti Māori with issues facing Māori.

National and Labour are rated the equal best parties to take care of defence / foreign affairs.

The only issue that saw a significant increase in concern was race relations/racism, at 6 percent, placed 13th equal - up from 16th equal in May.

The study was conducted using online research panels between 8 and 14 July 2026, with 1002 New Zealanders aged 18 and older taking part.

World.title: Paid firefighters to strike for one hour at midday on Friday
World.content:
Firefighters will be walking off the job for the 50th time since bargaining with Fire and Emergency New Zealand (FENZ) began in 2024.

Members of the New Zealand Professional Firefighters Union (NZPFU) will go on strike for one hour, from 12pm to 1pm, on Friday.

Secretary Wattie Watson said their members had not had a pay increase since July 2023.

That is despite FENZ having offered an increase of 2.4 percent for non-union members earlier this month.

Watson said it was an unprecedented level of industrial action in New Zealand, but was needed due to union busting and retaliatory action from FENZ.

In a statement, deputy national commander Megan Stiffler said it remained focused on achieving a fair and sustainable settlement with the NZPFU, "so we can continue working to keep communities safe".

Watson said the only offer made by FENZ was in July 2025, which offered 2 percent for 12 months from the date a deal was ratified, and 1.5 percent for each of the two following years.

However, Stiffler said the offer would have had a 2.2 percent increase from December 2025, and 2 percent from January 2027 over a 24-month term to the end of November 2027.

The offer would have cost $50 million over four years, Stiffler added, whereas NZPFU's settlement proposal was for more than $130m over the same period.

"We continue to call on the NZPFU to call off these reckless strikes while we remain engaged with the Employment Relations Authority (ERA) to try and come to a resolution," Stiffler said.

Stiffler said the ERA had proposed both FENZ and the NZPFU to exchange their full revised bargaining positions at the same time, to help assess whether further facilitation was likely to assist, but NZPFU refused.

Watson said that NZPFU had been clear that it wanted to return to bargaining, but after more than 50 days of negotiations, there was no point unless FENZ was going to make a new offer.

FENZ to prioritise emergencies

FENZ warned that it would prioritise emergencies, and may not attend less serious incidents, during the one-hour strike.

Stiffler said all 111 calls would be received and responded to, and it had an arrangement with Hato Hone St John and the Wellington Free Ambulance for medical events in impacted areas.

"However, our response times will be delayed in impacted areas as volunteer crews will be responding from the next closest location. So, we are asking the public to remain extra careful."

World.title: Ex-MAFS star Ridge Barredo sticking to weightlifting despite ugly injury
World.content:
Ridge Barredo's description of the knee injury that ended his Commonwealth Games weightlifting campaign is enough to turn most of us off even watching the sport for good.

"I heard it pop on the third attempt, I tried to give it my all and I heard it pop [out] and pop back in," he said of his failed third snatch attempt in the men's 110kg class.

"Just to feel it was a little bit scary. Initial pain was an eight or nine out of 10."

Barredo said it was the first time he had ever experienced an injury like that, sustained as he tried to throw 162 kilograms over his head.

Loading Instagram content

By the time he spoke to media, having been helped off the Armadillo stage, he said he was just "a little bit uncomfortable" and described the pain as down to a six or seven out of 10.

This was his third Commonwealth Games and the 30-year-old vowed to be back at Amdavad in four years.

"It's not the end. I'm still relatively young, still hungry for it, still want to be the best in Australia," he said.

"I'm not done yet, no way. Not a chance. I'll be back for sure. Four times, watch, mark my words."

And he said this difficult and painful journey is still preferable to a return to the scene that made his descriptor on Google not "athlete" or "weightlifter", but "internet personality".

That's thanks to his turn on reality TV show Married At First Sight three years ago.

One of only a handful of successful couples from the program, Barredo and wife Jade are still together.

Loading Instagram content

Jade and daughter Victoria were in the crowd watching as he suffered his injury.

And while the program worked out for him, Barredo says his TV days are over.

"My TV career is definitely done, I've found my partner. I'm off reality TV. Wouldn't recommend it," he said.

"If you want to have some fun in a toxic environment, go for it, but personally I wouldn't be going back."

He's not the only Games athlete shunning the reality TV scene (for now) with Scottish swimmer Katie Shanahan revealing she had to make a choice to continue swimming or go on Love Island last year.

'If you've got a lane, you've got a chance' An unexpected source kicks off another record-breaking night for Australian swimming as we get implicit and explicit reminders that we shouldn't take this for granted.

Shanahan opted not to enter the villa, ultimately winning silver in the women's 200m backstroke on the first night of the Glasgow swimming program.

"I'm the biggest Love Island fan ever. I've watched every season," Shanahan told BBC Scotland.

"Last year the producers asked me and [English swimmer] Abbie Wood if we would be interested in doing it.

"I couldn't go on, though, because [I was] focusing on the swimming, but who knows in the future?

"I was a bit tempted but the swimming had to come first."

World.title: 'Try not to die': Why Glasgow's gales hit different for hurdlers
World.content:
After rain blighted the first six days of the Commonwealth Games, Glasgow dialled up the dimmer on Thursday morning.

But a gorgeous, sunny, slightly brisk morning turned blustery and bleak by the time athletics competition was in full swing at Scotstoun Stadium.

It mercifully stayed dry as day seven's heats and qualifiers kicked off, but the wind was wreaking havoc across the track and field.

Australian javelin thrower Cameron McEntyre was launching into a mighty headwind that saw none of the 17 throwers reach the qualification standard of 84 metres.

The temperature plummeted as clouds rolled over Scotstoun. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

McEntyre got through on his 78.91m effort, but Kenya's Julius Yego, boasting the fourth longest throw in the Commonwealth this year, missed out on qualifying for the final as he finished in 13th spot.

"Everyone struggled with the wind and the temperature as well. Hopefully better conditions tomorrow and then push for a podium [but] everyone's in the same boat," McEntyre said, crediting his thorough preparation at training for keeping him ready for a day like today.

"If it's pissing down with rain or huge headwinds, whatever the conditions are, we just deal with it because we know one day there's gonna be a competition that's exactly the same."

And while hurling a spear into a breeze that's trying to throw it back at you might sound like the more dangerous prospect, Michelle Jenneke said her 100m hurdles with the wind at her back is a frightening experience.

Michelle Jenneke said the tailwind can mess up hurdlers' all-important stride patterns. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

"I get pretty jealous when I see the sprinters because you get a tailwind and you run fast, we get a tailwind and we're like 'let's try not to die today'. The hurdles were really coming at us," Jenneke said.

"I am just really really grateful we knew that was going to be a possibility and we really trained for it. It was tough today, towards the end I was really struggling to make sure I was hitting my stride pattern. But I think I did it really well, I did really safe and still managed to run quite fast."

Aussies on fire on a night when that should've been impossible Australian athletics lives up to the immense hype on a night of glorious culmination for Lachie Kennedy, Torrie Lewis and their team of track stars.

Jenneke clocked a time of 12.72 seconds, 0.05 of a second outside her personal best from two years ago, but this time with an illegal +4.3 metres per second tailwind.

"The wind was really pushing us onto the hurdles, it was a good time, though," she said after progressing to the evening's final as the sixth-fastest qualifier.

"Hopefully a little less windy [in the final] but I did really prepare for that tailwind and I think I handled it better than some of the other athletes."

Adeyah Brewster (background) went down at the final hurdle. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

She certainly did, with Barbados's Adeyah Brewster clipping the final hurdle and falling flat on her belly barely 6 metres short of the finish line.

National 400m champion Reece Holder experienced both sides of the coin in his single-lap semifinal, saying it was exactly what they expected when coming to Glasgow.

Aussies on fire on a night when that should've been impossible Australian athletics lives up to the immense hype on a night of glorious culmination for Lachie Kennedy, Torrie Lewis and their team of track stars.

"Everyone's running in the same conditions, so can't really complain because everyone's showing up to show out," he said.

Holder, who suffered a hamstring injury in mid-May, missed the 400m final while teammate Tom Reynolds won his semifinal to progress.

"I actually only just put spikes on two weeks ago from May," he said.

"So to come out here and run 45s, just be thankful for that and push forward for the future.

"I just don't think I'm race fit. Big ups to everyone else out there putting on a show for everyone in these conditions, but I just don't think I was there."

World.title: Roosters put up 82 points for highest NRL score in 91 years
World.content:
Sydney Roosters sent a warning to the rest of the NRL about their premiership credentials with a 82-12 whipping of North Queensland in Townsville, the most points by a winning team in 91 years.

Halfback Sam Walker, in the midst of a multi-million dollar contract negotiation, showed why Roosters supremo Nick Politis wants to keep him at the club for life in a masterclass display.

This was a muscle flex of epic proportions as the visitors scored the equal most first half points in premiership history to lead 48-6 after 40 minutes.

The Roosters scored eight first half tries with fullback James Tedesco and Walker both crossing twice. Walker's 24 points in the first half, including eight goals from as many attempts, was also the equal most points by an individual in an opening 40 minutes.

The team total of 82 was the most by a team since the Roosters beat Canterbury 87-7 in 1935. It was also the third-highest in premiership history.

Walker finished with 36 individual points and a hat-trick of tries, as did unstoppable winger Mark Nawaqanitawase.

Tedesco left the field at halftime with an ankle injury in a concern for the Tricolours.

North Queensland were helpless before the Tricolour onslaught. (Getty Images: Ian Hitchcock )

The Roosters temporarily joined Penrith on 34 competition points at the top of the table in their most complete performance of the season.

It was their sixth win in a row and a sign that come September they will be in prime position to challenge their bogey team Penrith.

The Cowboys are hanging on in eighth position but will drop back to ninth if Canterbury beat Melbourne away on Friday night.

The nature of the thrashing will test Cowboys coach Todd Payten's ability to get an appropriate response

Captain Tedesco, fresh from a hat-trick of tries last week, started and finished the opening try and it was carnage from that moment.

Roosters forwards Naufahu Whyte and Salesi Foketi monstered the hosts early and the spine of Tedesco, Daly Cherry-Evans, Walker and Reece Robson ran riot.

Tedesco, also the NSW custodian, is making a compelling case to oust Reece Walsh from the fullback position for Australia at the World Cup later in the year.

The Cowboys levelled at six-all when halves Jake Clifford and Jaxon Purdue combined to put Braidon Burns over but that was the only moment the match was in the balance.

A brilliant interchange of passing between halfback Walker and Tedesco led to the No.7 slicing over.

Tedesco then laid on a try for centre Hugo Savala with a left-foot grubber and it was clear which way the match was heading. . Walker's left foot step on the last tackle to score his second was elite.

The dazzling half set up runaway Foketi for a 40m rampage to the line.

The last try of the match, scored by replacement fullback Cody Ramsey, featured Walker grubbering and then kicking the ball over the head of the last dismal line of Cowboys defence.

AAP
