Tech.title: Private Claude Conversations Have Been Indexed by Search Engines
Tech.content:
Over the weekend, private Claude AI chats were made publicly accessible by search engines like Google and Bing, making for a privacy nightmare for the people involved and the chatbot’s maker, Anthropic.

Privacy concerns surrounding AI have always been around, but as these tools become more capable of pushing into your daily workflow with agentic capabilities, the threat of private data exposure is more timely than ever. This latest example shows that even simply sharing a conversation with others can get it exposed to a significantly larger audience.

This latest example shows that even simply sharing a conversation with others can get it exposed to a significantly larger audience.

Initially spotted by Reddit users, the common factor in the problem seems to be that the indexed conversations were shared — a common option within most AI chats — allowing “anyone with the link” to view what had been said in the Claude conversation itself.

This feature is apparently not completely protected from web crawlers, and personal conversations, while initially shared by users with people they chose, were exposed for the entire internet to see if one knew where to look.

Conversations indexed included medical records, sensitive personal information, internal corporate data and explicit content. They could be viewed within Google and Bing with a simple search and adding “site:claude.ai/share” to the query, yielding a trove of conversations, most of which have since been removed. Artifacts — tools, visualizations and shareable apps — were also accessible through search engines.

This isn’t the first time this has happened: Last year, Forbes reported the same thing happened with Anthropic — hundreds of conversations appeared on Google search results, only for them to be scrubbed later.

An Anthropic spokesperson told CNET that its system is working as it should and that when people decide to share their conversations, they’re making them publicly accessible.

“Shareable links are not guessable or discoverable unless people choose to share them themselves,” the spokesperson said. “When someone shares a conversation, they are making that content publicly accessible, and like other public web content, it may be archived by third-party services.”

Glenn Gabe, an SEO and AI search consultant at G-Squared Interactive, explained to CNET how this likely happened. It involves a .txt file called robots.txt, which is attached to the root of the website and contains directives about what bots can crawl and what they can’t. Gabe says some companies don’t understand how Google and Bing treat URLs being blocked by robots.txt, despite Google’s developer documents explaining the functionality of the file.

“If you block Google or Bing from crawling your content, they can still index those URLs, just without crawling the content,” Gabe says. Without crawling a page’s content, search engines also can’t see any directives in the HTML. “That’s why noindexing URLs that are blocked by robots.txt doesn’t make any sense.”



Gabe says that if a company had public URLs — like shared Claude chats — Anthropic should “noindex” the content and not block crawling via robots.txt. That way, while the content would still be on the web, it wouldn’t be indexed by search engines, and only the people with the specific link would be able to find the shared chats.

If ever there were a good time to adjust your privacy settings and delete old conversations from your go-to AI chatbot, it’s now. To view your shared chats in Claude, you can go to Settings > Privacy > Shared Chats.

Correction, July 30: Clarified the purpose of robots.txt files.

Tech.title: Most Smart Fitness Devices Lack Essential Data Protection, EFF Warns
Tech.content:
When it comes to protecting data collected by smart devices such as smartwatches and fitness bands, the Electronic Frontier Foundation is cautioning that most of the companies aren’t closing their rings on privacy.

In the report, “Most Smart Watches, Rings, and Bands Lack Basic Transparency Reports and Key Privacy Features,” the digital civil liberties group looked at several of the leading companies making smart health devices to see which ones had strong privacy policies over some of customers’ most sensitive data.

The EFF breaks its reporting into two distinct areas: how transparent companies are about law enforcement requests for the information, and whether the data is end-to-end encrypted between the device and the company collecting and processing it.

The results aren’t encouraging. Only a few companies are open about when data is shared, and only one thoroughly secures the data in a way that the company itself would not be able to access it.

Transparency about law enforcement access to your health data

The government can make official demands – through a subpoena or search warrant, for example – or unofficial requests for sensitive data collected by devices. For fitness trackers, that can reveal information such as a person’s location along with their heart rate at a certain point in time.

Just two companies, Apple and Google, publish transparency reports, with a third, Whoop, promising to notify users of such requests in public documentation. Oura has committed to issuing transparency reports in the future.

Thorin Klosowski, the article’s author and a security and privacy activist at the EFF, told CNET in an email, “I was a little surprised that so few companies publish transparency reports, and I hope that changes in the future, since we know a lot of them have data request options for law enforcement.”

One company uses end-to-end encryption of health data

A smart device like a watch or ring constantly collects data, not just when you’re in the middle of a workout. Analyzing information such as heart rate and respiration, particularly at night while you’re sleeping, can surface signs of possible health issues like sleep apnea.

That sensitive data is often moved to cloud storage to be synced and backed up to the company’s app on your phone. EFF spotlights end-to-end encryption in the article as a way to protect it from data intrusions or improper access by the company.

Apple touted its privacy work at its online WWDC event for developers. Apple/Screenshot by Stephen Shankland/CNET

The only company that passed this bar was Apple, which encrypts Apple Watch-collected data in the Health app in such a way that even it cannot read the details. The EFF noted that this is limited to the built-in Health app, and not third-party apps that collect and sync similar data.

“I knew that end-to-end encryption was super rare,” Klosowski wrote in his email, “but was also pretty disappointed at how few offer any sort of offline mode of any kind, let alone a full featured one. That’s one of those kind of ‘easy wins’ that I think would really benefit users.”

An Apple representative didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

The EFF article noted that companies offer encryption in transit and on device, but they can still see and use the data. “This is the industry standard, but it doesn’t have to be,” it reads.

Although end-to-end encryption is what the EFF hopes would be the standard, a few companies that responded to a request for comment from CNET reiterated that they take the privacy of customers’ data seriously.

The wrist-based Whoop 5.0 health tracker Nasha Addarich Martínez/CNET

A representative for Whoop responded via email with a link to the company’s privacy policy and wrote, “We protect member data, and members ultimately control their data. We use data to deliver Whoop, improve the product, and help members better understand their health. We have a pro-member data policy. We believe the individual owns the data, and we are not in the business of selling member data to advertisers.”

Similarly, a representative from Coros replied via email that, “We handle all personal information in full compliance with applicable international standards, including the EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and US laws. We maintain strict controls over data transfers, ensuring that customer details — including identifiers, metrics related to physiology, and activity data — are never sold to third parties. We are also dedicated to continually testing and updating our products to ensure that we use the most current security technology and approaches.” The rep also linked to the Coros privacy policy.

Oura’s representative said via email that the company does not sell or rent members’ personal information. “Members are in control of third-party integrations and can disconnect them at any time,” they wrote, “and we use technical and organizational safeguards to keep data safe and secure, including measures such as encryption, strict access controls, and anonymization or pseudonymization where appropriate.”

The Oura Ring 4 has a titanium exterior and interior. Carly Marsh/CNET

Garmin also pointed to its own privacy policies when contacted by CNET.

CNET Senior Editor for Health and Home Anna Gragert, who has used and reviewed many such smart devices, said it’s important that customers don’t automatically hit that agree button when presented with company policies.

“Wearable technology has been produced at a rate at which scientific research has had trouble catching up, so there aren’t enough studies looking into the potential downsides of these devices,” she said. “As a result, I think many consumers approach these wearables without fully understanding the possible risks, especially regarding privacy.”

CNET reached out to the other companies mentioned in the EFF article, but representatives didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.

The EFF article highlighted alternatives like keeping personal data encrypted on the device or synced phone, and processing it locally. That still delivers the insights that these types of wearables are touting without exposing the data. However, some models remain limited in that type of capability.

“We had a pretty good idea of the landscape, but still hoped it would turn out better than it did,” Klosowski said.

Tech.title: LinkedIn Added a New Way to Report AI Slop
Tech.content:
If you’re tired of reading obviously AI-generated LinkedIn posts about the magic of B2B sales, there’s hope: LinkedIn on Thursday released a new tool that allows you to report posts as “Seems like AI slop.”

AI slop is the term given to the deluge of posts, images and videos created with generative AI flooding social media like an oil spill. These posts tend to offer little value and clog up feeds. Every social media platform is struggling to hold back the tide of AI slop, and LinkedIn is certainly no exception.

A recent report from research firm Pangram found that one in four long-form social media posts was AI-generated. Of those AI posts, nearly two-thirds (62%) appeared on LinkedIn. On X (formerly Twitter), nearly half of all articles contained AI writing.

Now, you can report posts you’re suspicious of by tapping the three dots next to a post and selecting “Seems like AI slop.”

Screenshot by Katelyn Chedraoui/CNET

404 Media first spotted the feature. Hari Srinivasan, LinkedIn’s chief product officer, shared on Thursday that the company is ramping up efforts to identify AI slop. Allowing people to report posts that seem like AI slop will help LinkedIn get better at spotting the AI-created, low-quality content.

“Slop is hard to define and the definition changes; this lets us tune our models and make better feeds,” Srinivasan said.

It has also removed the “enhance with AI” option that appears when you are drafting a post, and will be replacing it with an option that proofreads your words without substantially rewriting them with AI. Srinivasan said LinkedIn is flagging “hundreds of thousands of automated comment attempts” and has blocked billions more attempts to use automated postings (usually with the aid of AI) across the platform.

Tech.title: Study: Switching From a Gas Stove to Electric Can Improve Asthma
Tech.content:
Can swapping from a gas to an electric stove help your asthma symptoms? Jena Ardell/Getty Images

When it comes to the gas vs. electric stove dispute, you’ll have people arguing about which is best for cooking and cookware and which is the safest, most affordable and most eco-friendly. A study published in early July about the health effects of gas stoves may contribute to this debate.

Conducted by the MetroHealth System, a Northeast Ohio hospital and academic medical center, in collaboration with six community organizations, the study found that participants with asthma reported improvements in their symptoms after switching from gas to electric stoves.

According to one of the researchers, Dr. Ashwini Sehgal, a professor of medicine at Case Western Reserve University, in an article published by the nonprofit news organization The Conversation, this is the first study to explore whether switching from a gas to an electric stove can reduce asthma symptoms.

What the study found

The study included 85 adults and children in Northeast Ohio with “poorly controlled asthma,” which was based on their symptoms, use of emergency medication and activity limitations. Each participant logged this information not only one to four weeks before their gas stoves were replaced at no cost with electric induction models, but also two to three months after the replacement.

“We chose electric induction stoves because they heat up and cool down rapidly, and they are safer and easier to clean than electric coil stoves,” Sehgal wrote in his The Conversation article. While induction stoves use an electromagnetic field to heat your cookware, electric stoves rely on electricity to do so.

Before and after the stoves were replaced, air quality monitors were used to measure nitrogen dioxide levels for seven-day periods. Nitrogen dioxide, a gaseous air pollutant emitted by gas stoves, can harm the lungs.

After the switch from gas to electric, indoor nitrogen dioxide levels decreased by 70%, and according to Sehgal, participants’ asthma symptoms went from moderate to mild, demonstrating improvements “similar to — or even greater than — those reported in clinical trials of commonly used asthma medications.”

Missed days of work or school decreased by about 80%, while ER visits and hospitalizations decreased by 70%.

Aside from asthma improvement, 98% of participants reported feeling satisfied or very satisfied with their new electric induction stoves, whereas 41% felt the same about their previous gas models.

An induction stove uses electricity, not gas, to work. Juan Algar/Getty Images

The study’s limitations

Sehgal notes that the study followed only a small number of people for a few months and did not include a comparison group with gas stoves. The results were also based on a self-reported questionnaire rather than medical records.

Results may not apply to people with mild asthma or to other US regions with different nitrogen dioxide levels.

Information wasn’t collected on other household sources of nitrogen dioxide, such as fireplaces or kerosene heaters, nor was data on participants’ allergy status, stove usage or additional medications.

As a result, further research is needed to confirm the study’s findings and to better understand long-term outcomes.

Researchers weren’t able to increase the study’s sample size or duration because the Trump administration terminated the project in May 2025, after it was selected for three years of funding by the US Environmental Protection Agency in December 2024.

Important considerations

As Sehgal put it in his article, switching from a gas stove to an electric one will not cure asthma or serve as a replacement for medical care and other health precautions.

It should also be considered that replacing a stove may not be financially feasible for many. “Most of our study participants lived in homes that were built before 1960, and we spent an average of $7,000 per household to upgrade their electrical systems as part of the study,” wrote Sehgal, adding that an electric stove plus installation costs about $1,500 in newer US homes.

If you have a gas stove, make sure you use the range hood’s exhaust fan to reduce airborne pollutants inside your home. Nattawat Jindamaneesirikul/Getty Images

What other stove research shows

Gas stoves are a source of indoor air pollution, as they emit gaseous pollutants, including nitrogen dioxide, carbon monoxide and volatile organic compounds such as benzene and formaldehyde, both of which can cause cancer.

A May 2024 study found that nitrogen dioxide, in particular, is produced by gas stoves in the US at short-term exposure levels higher than those deemed safe by both the US Environmental Protection Agency and the World Health Organization.

The 2024 study also estimated that, at the time, 50,000 cases of childhood asthma were linked to nitrogen dioxide emitted by gas stoves. If other gas stove pollutants were included, that number could rise to about 200,000 cases. Nitrogen dioxide has also been connected to lung cancer, diabetes, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and preterm birth.

Along with increased levels of particulate matter and sulfur dioxide, the American Lung Association reports that nitrogen dioxide has been linked to cancer, autoimmune disorders, pregnancy and birth outcomes and harm to the heart, lungs, kidneys and nervous system.

The University of California, Davis, Environmental Health Science Center adds that both electric and gas cooking can release PM2.5 (particles with a diameter of 2.5 microns or less) and ultrafine particles, which can cause or worsen respiratory conditions and increase the risk for cardiovascular disease, neurological disorders and immune system dysfunction.

In fact, frying foods on electric stoves produced higher particulate matter levels than on gas stoves.

However, it should be noted that gas stove pollutant levels can vary from home to home and that health effects will depend on these levels and the length of exposure. One’s lifestyle, health, age and current medical conditions can also determine health effects.

How to reduce indoor cooking air pollution

If you’re unable to switch from a gas to an electric stove, you can take other steps to reduce indoor air pollution when cooking. When outdoor air pollution is low, increase ventilation by opening windows and using your range hood’s exhaust.

If that isn’t feasible, consider purchasing an air purifier for your kitchen, which can filter out cooking particles and, if it includes an activated carbon filter, some gases, such as VOCs. Just make sure you regularly replace your air purifier’s filter so it works as intended, as it can spit pollutants back into your home if it becomes saturated.

At the end of the day, while replacing your gas stove with an electric model can reduce indoor air pollution and its health effects, it isn’t a complete solution. There are other steps you can take to improve your air quality.
